期應天府臣以例請

執事咸循典以充綜畫既密防
範惟嚴乃合諸曹六館暨提學
御史臣馮天馭所選士三試之登

punctuated:
應天府鄉試錄序

皇上臨御之二十有五年，維鄉貢之期，應天府臣以例請。上命侍讀臣朴、右中允臣陛往典試事。至，則同考學正臣謐、臣來鳳、臣民量、臣暠，教諭臣守道、臣文澤、臣廷桂、臣嘉績偕集。提調則府尹臣應奎、府丞臣鑰，監試則御史臣丕顯、臣一右。諸執事咸循典以充，綜畫旣密，防範惟嚴。乃合諸曹六館曁提學御史臣馮天馭所選士，三試之，登其雋及文之式者，成錄以獻。臣朴宜序諸簡端，用告于多士。

夫才賢之生，不偶然也，關諸氣
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination

In the twenty-fifth year of His Majesty’s reign, when the provincial tribute examination fell due, the officials of Yingtian Prefecture submitted a request in accordance with precedent. His Majesty commanded your servants Pu, Expositor-in-Waiting, and Bi, Right Mentor, to go and preside over the examination. Upon their arrival, the Associate Examiners assembled: School Instructors Mi, Laifeng, Minliang, and Gao, and Instructors Shoudao, Wenze, Tinggui, and Jiaji. The Proctors were Prefect Yingkui and Assistant Prefect Yue; the officials overseeing the examination were Censors Pixian and Yiyou. All the functionaries performed their duties according to established regulations. The overall arrangements were meticulous, and precautions were strict. They then assembled the candidates from the various government offices and the Six Colleges, together with those selected by the Censor for the Supervision of Education, Feng Tianyu, and examined them in three sessions. They entered the outstanding candidates and those compositions suitable to serve as models into a record for presentation to the throne. It falls to your servant Pu to place a preface at the beginning of this volume, addressing the assembled scholars.

The emergence of talented and worthy men is no mere accident; it is bound up with the vital forces …

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
運之昌隆發于山川之靈秀成
於教化之潤漬惟我
皇朝驅胡蕩氛闢夏立極寔當
天啓之期清淑醇龐之氣凝萃翕閼
者悉宣融而暢達肆人文昭朗
品彙嘉途媲古煕和其氣運不
旣昌隆矣乎惟南畿爲
===
今豐芑之遺古所稱
帝王之宅者也龍蟠虎踞孕靈而發
祥北聯兗豫南控楚越江山環
匯沃衍千里苞篚舟車之
貢甲天下其山川不旣靈秀矣乎
惟
祖宗弘文右儒先後一揆遐陬僻壤

今豐芑之遺古所稱
帝王之宅者也龍蟠虎踞孕靈而發
祥北聯兗豫南控楚越江山環
匯沃衍千里苞篚舟車之
貢甲天下其山川不旣靈秀矣乎
惟
祖宗弘文右儒先後一揆遐陬僻壤
punctuated: 運之昌隆，發于山川之靈秀，成於教化之潤漬。惟我皇朝驅胡蕩氛，闢夏立極，寔當天啓之期。清淑醇龐之氣，凝萃翕閼者，悉宣融而暢達。肆人文昭朗，品彙嘉途，媲古煕和，其氣運不旣昌隆矣乎？惟南畿爲今豐芑之遺，古所稱帝王之宅者也。龍蟠虎踞，孕靈而發祥，北聯兗豫，南控楚越，江山環匯，沃衍千里，苞篚舟車之貢甲天下，其山川不旣靈秀矣乎？惟祖宗弘文右儒，先後一揆，遐陬僻壤，
translation_en:
…the flourishing of the cosmic cycles; it springs from the numinous beauty of mountains and rivers and is brought to maturity through the permeating influence of moral instruction. Our imperial dynasty drove out the Hu, swept away their baleful influence, opened up the Chinese realm, and established the supreme standard of rule, truly at a time when Heaven opened the way. The pure, beneficent, rich, and abundant vital energies, previously concentrated and pent up, were all released into harmonious and unimpeded circulation. Thus human culture shone brightly, and all kinds of beings followed auspicious paths [?], matching the radiant harmony of antiquity. Were not its cosmic cycles indeed flourishing?
The Southern Metropolitan Region preserves today the legacy of the luxuriant qi plants celebrated in the ode Feng shui [?]; it is what the ancients called the dwelling place of emperors and kings. With a dragon coiled and a tiger crouching, it nurtures numinous powers and brings forth auspicious signs. To the north it adjoins Yan and Yu; to the south it commands Chu and Yue. Rivers and mountains encircle and converge upon it, and its fertile plains extend a thousand li. Its tribute, packed in bundles and baskets and conveyed by boat and cart, ranks foremost in the realm. Are not its mountains and rivers indeed endowed with numinous beauty?
Our imperial ancestors promoted literary culture and honored Confucian scholars, following one consistent standard from reign to reign; in distant corners and secluded regions…

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
德一俗同我
皇上道隆
君師制兼述作闡
敬一秩
典禮菁莪棫樸之化覃洽海宇黌
序俊髦咸彬彬郁郁稱先王而
遵古昔其教化不既潤賁矣乎
===
夫運言乎其際也靈言乎其毓
也化言乎其被也三者會而才
賢之生於斯爲盛矣乃今典試
猶夙夜惴惴恒以弗得才賢莫
能仰稱
德意是懼何也譬諸木焉蒲楊樸
樕非不蔚然茂也匠氏過而弗
alt_text:
德一俗同我
皇上道隆
君師制彝述作闡
敬一秩
典禮菁莪棫樸之化覃洽海宇亹
序俊髦咸彬彬郁郁稱先王而
遵古昔其教化不既潤〔貴矣乎〕
===
大運言乎其際也靈言乎其毓
也化言乎其被也三者會而才
賢之生於斯爲盛矣乃今與試
猶夙夜惴惴恒以弗得才賢莫
能仰稱
德意是懼何也譬諸木焉蒲楊樸
樕非不蔚然茂也匠氏過而弗
punctuated:
德一俗同。我皇上道隆君師，制兼述作，闡敬一，秩典禮，菁莪棫樸之化覃洽海宇，黌序俊髦咸彬彬郁郁，稱先王而遵古昔，其教化不既潤賁矣乎？
夫運言乎其際也，靈言乎其毓也，化言乎其被也。三者會，而才賢之生於斯爲盛矣。乃今典試，猶夙夜惴惴，恒以弗得才賢、莫能仰稱德意是懼，何也？譬諸木焉，蒲楊樸樕非不蔚然茂也，匠氏過而弗
translation_en:
…virtue is unified and customs are alike. Our Emperor embodies in the highest degree the Way of ruler and teacher; his institutions combine the transmission of inherited traditions with new creation. He elucidates reverent single-mindedness and sets the canonical rites in order. His transforming influence, like that celebrated in “Luxuriant Mugwort” (Jing e) and “The Oaks” (Yu pu), extends throughout the realm. The outstanding scholars of the schools all display refined accomplishment and abundant cultivation, extolling the former kings and following antiquity. Has his moral instruction not richly nourished and adorned them?
Now, fortune concerns the conjunction of circumstances; numinous potency concerns the nurturing of talent; moral transformation concerns the reach of its influence. These three converge, and talented and worthy men consequently arise here in abundance. Yet those now presiding over the examination remain apprehensive day and night, constantly fearing that they will fail to find talented and worthy men and thus be unable to fulfill His Majesty’s virtuous intentions. Why is this? Consider trees: willows, poplars, and scrub oaks certainly grow luxuriantly, yet the craftsman passes by and does not…

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
眎干霄合抱之材則皇皇是求
陟高歷險弗憚且止者爲其直
大而適于用也多士行將登諸
用矣盍以直大者自期乎古稱
人之不朽固曰立德立功立言
矣夫德必當世而章功宜乘時
而顯言乃功德之餘也方今
===
聖主當陽羣賢彙征矢謨宣力懋庸
樹勛眞千載一時也多士玆以
文薦亦可謂良于言矣其圖務
德與功乎庶幾楨
王國棟
明堂如干霄合抱用途其直且大
者其於

眎。干霄合抱之材，則皇皇是求，陟高歷險，弗憚且止者，爲其直大而適于用也。多士行將登諸用矣，盍以直大者自期乎？古稱人之不朽，固曰立德、立功、立言矣。夫德必當世而章，功宜乘時而顯，言乃功德之餘也。
方今聖主當陽，羣賢彙征，矢謨宣力，懋庸樹勛，眞千載一時也！多士玆以文薦，亦可謂良于言矣。其圖務德與功乎？庶幾楨王國，棟明堂，如干霄合抱，用途其直且大者，其於
translation_en:
…give them a glance. Yet timber that reaches into the clouds and takes two arms to encircle is sought with anxious eagerness: the carpenter climbs heights and traverses dangerous ground, undaunted and unwilling to stop [?], because it is straight, great, and suited to use. You scholars will soon advance into service. Why should you not aspire to such uprightness and greatness? The ancients spoke of human immortality as establishing virtue, achieving merit, and leaving enduring words. Virtue must shine forth in one’s own age; achievement should become manifest by seizing the opportunities of the time. Words are the further expression of achievement and virtue.
Now, with our sagely sovereign facing south in rule and worthy men advancing together, offering counsel and exerting their strength, accomplishing great services and establishing merit, this is truly an opportunity encountered once in a thousand years! You scholars have now been recommended on the strength of your writing, and may indeed be called accomplished in words. Will you not devote yourselves to virtue and achievement? Then you may become supporting posts of the royal realm and ridgepoles of the Hall of Enlightenment, like trees reaching into the clouds and requiring two arms to encircle, putting your uprightness and greatness to use [?]. title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
昌期靈秀
神化不益有明徵也哉主司期待
于多士者若此多士其勗諸
翰林院侍讀郭朴謹序
alt_text:
昌期靈秀
神化不益有明徵也哉主司期待
于多士者若此多士其勗諸
翰林院侍讀郭朴謹序
punctuated:
昌期靈秀、神化，不益有明徵也哉？主司期待于多士者若此，多士其勗諸！

翰林院侍讀郭朴謹序。
translation_en:
…would this not furnish still clearer evidence of the numinous excellence and divine transforming influence of this flourishing age? Such are the expectations that the presiding examiners hold for the assembled scholars. May you scholars exert yourselves!

Preface respectfully written by Guo Pu, Reader-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy.

translation_en:
Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination, twenty-fifth year of Jiajing (1546).

Proctors:
Jiang Yingkui, Prefect of Yingtian Prefecture, courtesy name Wenhuan, was from the Mayi Defense Battalion under the Shanxi Regional Military Commission. He became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in the bingxu year.
Li Yong, Grand Master of Central Compliance and Vice Prefect of Yingtian Prefecture, courtesy name Boyin, was from Quwo County, Shanxi. He became a metropolitan graduate in the bingxu year.

Examiners:
Guo Pu, Reader-in-waiting in the Hanlin Academy, courtesy name Zhifu, was from Anyang County, Henan. He became a metropolitan graduate in the yiwei year.
Sun Sheng, Right Companion in the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, courtesy name Zhigao, was registered with the Embroidered-uniform Guard and was from Yuyao County, Zhejiang. He became a metropolitan graduate in the yiwei year.

Associate Examiners:
Huang Mi, Instructor in the Confucian School of Zhao Subprefecture, Zhending Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, courtesy name Jingqing, was from Ruyang County, Henan. He attained gongshi status in the gengzi year.

第壹場

四書
孝者，所以事君也。
周監於二代，郁郁乎文哉！吾從周。
學問之道無他，求其放心而已矣。

易
復，其見天地之心乎！
君子之光，其暉吉也。
與天地相似，故不違；知周乎萬物，而道濟天下，故不過；旁行而不流，樂天知命，故不憂；安土敦乎仁，故能愛。
說萬物者，莫說乎澤；潤萬物者，莫潤乎水。

咨！汝二十有二人，欽哉！惟時亮天功。
說拜稽首曰：「敢對揚天子之休命。」
天惟純佑命，則商實。百姓王人，罔不秉德明恤；小臣屏侯甸，矧咸奔走。
寬而有制，從容以和。
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

Filial devotion is the means by which one serves one's ruler.

Zhou took the two preceding dynasties as its models. How splendid its culture! I follow Zhou.

The way of learning and inquiry is nothing other than seeking to recover one's wayward mind.

Book of Changes (Yi)

In Return, do we not see the heart of Heaven and Earth!

The light of the gentleman: its radiance is auspicious.

He accords with Heaven and Earth and therefore does not go against them. His knowledge encompasses the myriad things, and his Way benefits all under Heaven; therefore he does not err. He moves in all directions without going astray. He delights in Heaven and understands its mandate; therefore he has no anxiety. He is content where he dwells and steadfast in benevolence; therefore he can love.

Of things that gladden the myriad beings, none gladdens them more than the marsh; of things that moisten the myriad beings, none moistens them more than water.

Book of Documents (Shu)

Ah, you twenty-two men, be reverent! Assist in accomplishing Heaven's work.

Yue bowed and touched his head to the ground, saying: “I venture to acknowledge and extol the Son of Heaven's gracious command.”

Heaven bestowed its full support upon their mandate, and Shang was thereby strengthened. The officials of the various clans and the king's attendants all upheld virtue and exercised enlightened care. Even the lesser ministers served as bulwarks for the lords of the outer and inner domains—how much more those who hurried about in royal service.

Be generous yet maintain restraint, composed and harmonious.

translation_en:
Book of Odes

The cuckoo is in the mulberry tree; its young are seven. The good man, the gentleman, is constant in his bearing. Constant in his bearing, his heart is as firmly bound as a knot.

They are his screens and supports; the many lords take them as their model. Are they not harmonious and dignified? Are the blessings they receive not abundant?

Diligently our king orders and regulates the four quarters.

It is not merely now that this is so, nor did it begin today: it has been thus from remote antiquity.

Spring and Autumn Annals

In autumn, in the eighth month, on renwu, a grand military review was held. Sixth year of Duke Huan.

In summer, men of Qi attacked our northern borderlands. Twenty-sixth year of Duke Xi. In summer, the duke met the Marquis of Qi at Jiagu. The duke returned from Jiagu. Tenth year of Duke Ding.

In summer, in the fourth month, on xinsi, men of Jin and the Jiang Rong defeated Qin at Xiao. 〔Thirty-third year of Duke Xi.〕

In spring, in the second month according to the royal calendar, on jiazi, the Marquis of Jin fought the army of Qin at Pengya. The Qin army suffered a crushing defeat.

In winter, men of Jin, Song, Chen, and Zheng attacked Qin. 〔Both entries are from the second year of Duke Wen.〕 Men of Qin attacked Jin. Third year of Duke Wen.

In spring, in the second month according to the royal calendar, Jisun Si, Shusun Zhouqiu, and Zhongsun Heji led an army against Zhu and seized the lands east of the Huo and west of the Yi.

On guisi, Shusun Zhouqiu and Zhongsun Heji concluded a covenant with the Viscount of Zhu at Gouyi. Duke Ai …

Record of Rites (Liji)
Order the official in charge of rites to examine the seasons and months, determine the days, and harmonize the pitch pipes; rectify rites, music, institutions, measures, and dress.
Acting at the appropriate moment is called timeliness.
Great music shares the harmony of Heaven and Earth; great ritual shares their ordered rhythms. Through harmony, the myriad things retain their proper nature; through ordered rhythms, sacrifices are offered to Heaven and Earth. In the visible realm there are rites and music; in the unseen realm there are ghosts and spirits.
Ritual precedes gifts of silk because the intention is that the people should put service before emolument.

問：古昔帝王之興，必握正統以臨天下，攺正朔以一人心，載在簡編，班班可攷。正統、正朔之名，果何所昉與？歐陽脩著《正統論》，而蘇軾祖其說；葉時著《正朔解》，而蔡沈祖其說，可得聞與？作《通鑑綱目》者，進蜀漢、黜曹魏，爲得尊王之義，然君子有遺論焉。傳《春秋》者，斷以夏時冠周月，乃學者不能無疑，抑又何故與？昔人謂正統之說本乎《春秋》，正朔之善質諸孔
translation_en:
…in the rear hall of Yongming: a congratulatory memorial from the assembled officials.

Five legal judgments:
1. A fellow official renders judgments and signs case documents on another’s behalf.
2. A serving official erects a stele to himself without authorization.
3. Livestock are tended and raised contrary to the prescribed regulations.
4. Persons charged with making arrests pursue and apprehend offenders.
5. Someone hears that an amnesty has been granted and deliberately commits an offense.

Third Session
Five Policy Questions

Question: When the emperors and kings of antiquity rose to power, they invariably took hold of the legitimate succession to rule All Under Heaven and changed the calendrical system to unite the people’s hearts. These matters are recorded in the historical writings and can be clearly verified. Where, indeed, did the terms “legitimate succession” (zhengtong) and “calendrical system” (zhengshuo) originate? Ouyang Xiu wrote the Discourse on Legitimate Succession, and Su Shi based his views upon it; Ye Shi wrote the Explanation of the Calendrical System, and Cai Shen based his views upon it. May we hear an account of these views?

The author of the Outline and Details of the Comprehensive Mirror elevated Shu Han and excluded Cao Wei, thereby attaining the principle of honoring the rightful king; yet gentlemen have offered further critical observations on this. Commentators on the Spring and Autumn Annals have concluded that it places Xia seasonal designations before Zhou month designations, yet scholars cannot be free of doubt. Why is this so?

People of earlier times said that the theory of legitimate succession was grounded in the Spring and Autumn Annals, and that the soundness of a calendrical system should be tested against Confucius …

問古今言治理之術恒曰安內攘外不知
所謂安攘者其道亦相須否與夫安內
莫重乎教養攘外不出乎戰守今其法
固在也而民生未遂疆宇非寧其故何
與議者曰安內在擇吏吏良則教養舉
punctuated:
子，然與否與？我太祖高皇帝奮迹淮甸，再造中華，酌用夏時，永貽典則。正統正朔，比隆于唐虞三代，而漢唐宋不足論矣。肆我皇上以元聖之資，撫中興之運，鴻功峻德，莫可名言。至若撤祀胡元，翼統以扶人紀；冊稱上帝，崇朔以立天常，寔振古所希聞，皇祖所未備也。爾諸生涵濡聖化，亦既有年，其鋪張而揚厲之，以彰我國家之盛。

問：古今言治理之術，恒曰安內攘外。不知所謂安攘者，其道亦相須否與？夫安內莫重乎教養，攘外不出乎戰守。今其法固在也，而民生未遂，疆宇弗寧，其故何與？議者曰：「安內在擇吏，吏良則教養舉，
translation_en:
…Confucius—is this so or not? Our Emperor Taizu Gao rose to prominence in the Huai region and re-created Chinese civilization. He adopted the seasonal reckoning of the Xia with due deliberation, bequeathing enduring standards. In legitimate dynastic succession and calendrical ordering, his achievements equaled those of Tang Yao, Yu Shun, and the Three Dynasties; the Han, Tang, and Song cannot bear comparison. Now our reigning Emperor, endowed with the qualities of a supreme sage, presides over an era of restoration. His vast achievements and lofty virtue defy description. As for discontinuing sacrifices to the non-Chinese Yuan rulers, thereby upholding legitimate succession and sustaining the human order; and employing the designation “Sovereign on High” in the ceremonial text [?], thereby honoring calendrical authority and establishing Heaven’s constant order—these are indeed things rarely heard of since antiquity, which even his imperial ancestors had not fully accomplished. You students have been steeped in his sage transforming influence for years. Expound and extol these achievements, making manifest the grandeur of our dynasty.

Question: From antiquity to the present, those who discuss the arts of government invariably speak of securing peace within and repelling threats from without. Yet do the methods of this securing and repelling depend upon one another? In securing peace within, nothing is more important than educating and sustaining the people; repelling threats from without consists in warfare and defense. The requisite institutions certainly exist today, yet the people’s livelihoods remain unfulfilled and the realm is not at peace. Why is this? Some argue: “Securing peace within depends on selecting officials. If officials are capable, education and sustenance will be provided…”

translation_en:
…Repelling external threats depends on selecting generals: when the generals are worthy, warfare and defense are properly conducted. Is this so or not? Our dynasty selects prefects and magistrates with care and attaches great importance to the appointment of commanders. Throughout the interior, prefectures and counties all have civil officials; along the frontiers, the defense commands all have generals. Yet civil administration has not attained excellence, and military achievements have not been established. Men bear the titles of generals and civil officials, but few possess the corresponding substance. We seldom see men comparable to the worthy administrators of ancient Bohai, Yingchuan, Nanyang, and Shujun, or the outstanding commanders of Yunzhong, Huangzhong, Shangjun, and Shanggu. Is this because the talents of ancient and present times are not entirely alike? Or have the various offices failed to find the proper means of overseeing and encouraging them? If we now require prefects and magistrates to relieve the people's suffering, and commanders to rouse the soldiers' morale, can we thereby fully achieve internal peace and the repulsion of external threats? You candidates observe the times with deeply stirred hearts and surely have ways to address these matters. Please speak forthrightly, without holding back.

Question: Of the ways a scholar establishes himself in the world, none surpass learning and practical achievement. In learning, one must take Kongzi and Mengzi as teachers; in achievement, one must take Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou as standards. Across the thousand years and more since the Qin and Han, could there have been no such men? Why, then, have later generations so often criticized them? Let us take those whose deeds are clearly recorded in histories and biographies and assess them together with you candidates. One devoted himself to the great undertaking and dismissed the Hundred Schools; another lived in retirement teaching students, taking the traditions of the Zhu and Si rivers as the standard for his words; another repudiated heterodox teachings and exalted Master Meng. text:
可謂非學術矣其於孔孟之宗亦庶幾
否耶運籌決勝而佐成帝業隱臥應聘
而志匡王室潛授豪賢而卒正主器不
可謂非事功矣其於伊周之軌果無戾
否耶夫數子者翼聖輔世亦足以稱矣
而世儒每有訾言抑又何耶諸士素蘊
學術而以事功自期者必嘗詳考而明

可謂非學術矣。其於孔孟之宗，亦庶幾否耶？運籌決勝而佐成帝業，隱臥應聘而志匡王室，潛授豪賢而卒正主器，不可謂非事功矣。其於伊周之軌，果無戾否耶？夫數子者，翼聖輔世，亦足以稱矣，而世儒每有訾言，抑又何耶？諸士素蘊學術而以事功自期者，必嘗詳考而明辨之，願聞至當之論。

問：學以際天人爲大，故天道雖幽遠高深，不可不求其實。傳稱天文有二十一家，四百四十五卷，其槩可得聞與？天包於外，地凝於內，以分至啓閉定歲，以晦朔弦朢定月，以晨昏出沒定日。名察度數，別清濁，起五部，建氣物，紛錯理茫，籍浩，曷究其因？至謂七政性殊，恒星體靜，三垣中宅，列宿四垂，經星可以象占，緯星可以數測，常名可名，應官應事，微星奚啻千萬，覈往占來，歷示休咎，又曷鈞致
translation_en:
…cannot be said to fall outside learning. Yet did these attainments approach the central tradition of Confucius and Mencius? Some devised strategies that secured victory and helped establish an imperial enterprise; some answered a summons from retirement, intent on upholding the royal house; some privately instructed outstanding worthy men and ultimately secured the rightful succession. These cannot be denied the status of practical achievements. Yet were they indeed wholly consistent with the path of Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou? These men deserve praise for supporting the sages and aiding their age. Why, then, have later Confucian scholars repeatedly criticized them? You gentlemen, who have long cultivated learning and aspire to practical achievement, must surely have examined these matters closely and distinguished them clearly. We wish to hear your most judicious assessment.

Question: The highest concern of learning is to comprehend the relationship between Heaven and humanity. Thus, although the Way of Heaven is obscure and remote, lofty and profound, one must seek its underlying realities. The transmitted record states that writings on celestial patterns comprise twenty-one schools, in four hundred and forty-five scrolls. May we hear an outline of them? Heaven envelops the outside, while Earth coheres within. The equinoxes, solstices, and beginnings of the seasons determine the year; the last and first days of the lunar month, the quarter moons, and the full moon determine the month; dawn and dusk, rising and setting, determine the day. In naming and examining celestial measures, distinguishing the clear from the turbid, establishing the five divisions, and setting out vital forces and material phenomena [?], the intricacies are bewildering, the principles obscure, and the writings vast: how can their underlying causes be investigated? It is further said that the seven luminaries differ in nature, that the fixed stars are stationary in substance, that the Three Enclosures occupy the center, and that the constellations extend around the four quarters. The fixed stars permit prognostication through their configurations, and the planets can be measured by calculation. Those with established names can be named and correspond to offices and affairs; the faint stars number far more than thousands or myriads. By examining the past and forecasting the future, auspicious and inauspicious signs are successively disclosed. How, moreover, can one attain a comprehensive understanding of … [?]

translation_en:
…their laws and patterns? In antiquity, kings, princes, and lords reverently followed Heaven, taking its seasons as their rule: they established the calendrical starting point at the beginning, determined the proper sequence in the middle, and assigned the remainder at the end. Thus they handed down their great renown without limit. How could scholars and officials dismiss this learning as prophetic divination, using that pretext to abandon it without discussion? Please weigh the accounts in the classics and histories and set out your conclusions fully in your essay. This will not only test your learning concerning Heaven but also reveal the Way of serving Heaven.
Question: Moral instruction and social customs are major concerns of government. In the age of the former kings, virtue was unified and customs were shared; the transformation they brought about in its pristine simplicity has scarcely ever been equaled. In later ages, moral instruction was unclear and customs were improper. Even when men wished to speak of good government, everything amounted merely to expediency.
The sagely founder rose vigorously in accordance with the destined turn of events, swept away barbarian defilement, and strengthened and ordered the enduring human relationships. People then reformed their hearts and applied themselves diligently to virtue, and the lands in all four directions enjoyed great harmony. Successive sage emperors carried on this inheritance, tirelessly adapting to changing circumstances. Now our present Emperor has revitalized the dynasty and exerted himself with determination, extending moral transformation and clarifying human relationships. Through comprehensive regulation, the myriad people have received blessings [?], surpassing those of former times. Yet, as established practices have long continued, customs have diverged somewhat from those at the beginning. To enumerate the principal instances: official standards have gradually slackened, and official duties are neglected; learning has branched into divergent paths, and scholars’ conduct has become deviant; the dwellings of registered commoners exceed their proper station and observe no distinctions of rank; neighborhood gatherings are extravagant and squander wealth; clerks exploit the law to pursue private ends; and cunning men contrive lawsuits to obtain illicit profit. title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
孝者所以事君也
袁洪愈
同考試官教諭鄭批闡明子臣一道甚
眞切有關世教取之不獨以其文也
同考試官學正蘇批發揮家國一理之
意殆盡
考試官右中允孫批忠孝之意藹然
===
考試官侍讀郭批純雅明暢
傳者論子道通於臣道見家國之教同也夫道
一而已矣在子則為孝在臣則為忠豈以家國
而有異教也哉大學傳之九章釋齊家治國至
此蓋謂天下之不一者勢也其本始不一者理
也君子治國必觀于家亦惟以理之一耳何則
子之於親有孝道焉致愛致敬以敦一本之恩
用力用勞以昭罔極之德孰不曰此人子事親
之職無與於君也殊不知内則父子外則君臣

傳者論子道通於臣道，見家國之教同也。夫道一而已矣，在子則為孝，在臣則為忠，豈以家國而有異教也哉？大學傳之九章釋齊家治國，至此蓋謂天下之不一者，勢也；其本始不一者，理也。君子治國必觀于家，亦惟以理之一耳。何則？子之於親，有孝道焉。致愛致敬，以敦一本之恩；用力用勞，以昭罔極之德。孰不曰此人子事親之職，無與於君也？殊不知内則父子，外則君臣，
translation_en:
First Session
Four Books
“Filial piety is the means by which one serves the ruler.”
Yuan Hongyu

Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor, comments: “He elucidates the single Way shared by son and minister with great sincerity and precision. This bears upon moral instruction in the world; we select it for more than its literary merit alone.”
Associate Examiner Su, School Instructor, comments: “He develops almost exhaustively the idea that family and state share a single principle.”
Examiner Sun, Right Mentor of the Heir Apparent, comments: “The spirit of loyalty and filial piety is abundantly evident.”
Examiner Guo, Reader-in-Waiting, comments: “Pure and refined, lucid and fluent.”

The commentator discusses how the Way of the son extends to the Way of the minister, showing that the moral teaching of family and state is the same. The Way is simply one: in a son it is filial piety; in a minister it is loyalty. How could there be different teachings merely because one concerns the family and the other the state? Chapter Nine of the commentary on the Great Learning explains ordering the family and governing the state. At this point, it presumably means that what varies throughout the world is circumstance, while what varies at its very origin is principle [?]. When the gentleman governs the state, he must look to the family, solely because principle is one. Why is this? A son owes his parents the Way of filial piety. He offers the utmost love and respect to deepen the affection arising from their common source; he exerts his strength and labors to manifest their boundless beneficence. Who would not say that these are a son’s duties in serving his parents, with no connection to the ruler? Yet they fail to understand that within the household there are father and son, and outside it there are ruler and minister …

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
人紀天經均之爲不可易之分邇之事父遠之
事君凝承敬順均之有不容已之情明發不寐
之懷卽夙夜匪懈之念也移孝於忠乃同體而
異用竭盡其力之誠卽委質其身之義也遡忠
於孝寔因事而殊名能祗服以事親者必能靖
共以事君舉此心之眞切者而周旋焉濟世安
民之略在是矣能諭親以從道者必能引君於
當道由一念之惻怛者而時措焉責難陳善之
謨在是矣是何也父母者家之嚴君大君者民
===
之父母勢無間隔理寔相通世未有孝而後其
君亦未有忠而遺其親者也謂之曰孝者所以
事君亶其然乎事長之弟使衆之慈蓋可以類
推者而君子以是立教於家則國之觀感自有
不容已矣抑攷克諧之聖乃言底可績而翼翼
服事亦惟一日三朝問安視膳者能之傳曰求
忠於孝諒哉然立身行道揚名於後世又孝之
終也學者知孝所以爲忠則事親不容於不至
知忠所以爲孝則於事君可不益盡其誠乎交

punctuated: 人紀天經，均之爲不可易之分；邇之事父，遠之事君，凝承敬順，均之有不容已之情。明發不寐之懷，卽夙夜匪懈之念也；移孝於忠，乃同體而異用。竭盡其力之誠，卽委質其身之義也；遡忠於孝，寔因事而殊名。能祗服以事親者，必能靖共以事君，舉此心之眞切者而周旋焉，濟世安民之略在是矣。能諭親以從道者，必能引君於當道，由一念之惻怛者而時措焉，責難陳善之謨在是矣。是何也？父母者，家之嚴君；大君者，民之父母。勢無間隔，理寔相通。世未有孝而後其君，亦未有忠而遺其親者也。謂之曰「孝者，所以事君」，亶其然乎！事長之弟，使衆之慈，蓋可以類推者。而君子以是立教於家，則國之觀感自有不容已矣。抑攷克諧之聖，乃言底可績；而翼翼服事，亦惟一日三朝、問安視膳者能之。傳曰：「求忠於孝。」諒哉！然立身行道，揚名於後世，又孝之終也。學者知孝所以爲忠，則事親不容於不至；知忠所以爲孝，則於事君可不益盡其誠乎？交
translation_en:
…the bonds of human relations and the constant principles of Heaven alike impose duties that cannot be changed. Serving one’s father close at hand and serving one’s ruler farther afield, with solemn obedience and respectful compliance, alike involve feelings that cannot be suppressed. The concern that keeps one awake until dawn is precisely the resolve to remain diligent morning and night. To transfer filial devotion to loyalty is to give different applications to the same underlying substance. The sincerity with which one exhausts one’s strength for one’s parents is precisely the sense of duty with which one pledges oneself to one’s ruler. Tracing loyalty back to filial devotion reveals that their different names arise only from the different affairs to which they apply. One who can serve one’s parents reverently can surely serve one’s ruler with conscientious respect. By bringing this heartfelt sincerity to bear in one’s dealings, one possesses the means to aid the world and bring peace to the people. One who can persuade one’s parents to follow the Way can surely guide one’s ruler onto the proper Way. By applying this compassionate concern as circumstances require, one possesses the counsel needed to demand difficult achievements of the ruler and set goodness before him.

Why is this so? Parents are the august rulers of the household; the sovereign is the father and mother of the people. Their positions present no barrier between them, and their underlying principles are indeed connected. There has never been anyone who was filial yet put his ruler last, nor anyone who was loyal yet neglected his parents. How true, then, is the statement, “Filial devotion is the means by which one serves one’s ruler”! The deference with which one serves elders and the kindness with which one directs the multitude may likewise be inferred by analogy. When the gentleman establishes instruction in his household through these virtues, those in the state who observe him cannot help being moved.

Consider, moreover, the sage who brought his family into harmony: only then was it said that he could achieve success in office. And reverent service could likewise be rendered only by one who attended his parents three times each day, inquired after their well-being, and inspected their meals. The Commentary says, “Seek loyalty among the filial.” How trustworthy these words are! Yet establishing oneself, practicing the Way, and making one’s name renowned in later generations are also the culmination of filial devotion. If students understand that filial devotion is the means of being loyal, they cannot fail to serve their parents to the utmost. If they understand that loyalty is the means of being filial, can they fail to devote themselves still more sincerely to serving their ruler? Mutually…

周監于二代郁郁乎文哉吾從周

王制稽古而大備，聖人之所不能違也。夫稽古而損益之，王制之所爲備也。聖人之從之也，有以哉！想其意若曰：聖王之治天下也，不可變者，道也；而不相沿者，禮也。夏之尚忠，商之尚質，皆嘗卓然爲一代之憲矣。至於我周，文武具明聖之德，周公當制作之權。是故監于有夏，監于有商，本經綸之迹，以盡折衷之詳，而立乎當代之良法；損其太過，補其不及，因風氣之開，以繼先王之志，而集乎典禮之大成。愿而愨者，有文以濟之，品式章程，至詳至備，達天下於昭明之觀
translation_en:
…cultivate both and attain a profound understanding of them; only then will one be worthy of the Way of the Great Learning.

“Zhou took the two preceding dynasties as its models. How splendid its cultural refinement! I follow Zhou.”

Ma □

Associate Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: “The reasoning is clear and the form correct; the language is elegant and the ideas fresh. This is surely a splendid example of contemporary examination prose.”

Associate Examiner Chen, School Instructor, comments: “It brings out well the Master's intention in following Zhou.”

Examiner Sun, Right Mentor, comments: “Full-bodied and substantial.”

Examiner Guo, Reader-in-Waiting, comments: “Gentle and pure.”

Royal institutions, through examination of antiquity, attained full completeness: even the Sage could not depart from them. Indeed, examining antiquity and making appropriate reductions and additions were the means by which royal institutions became complete. There was good reason for the Sage to follow them! We may imagine his meaning as follows:

When sage kings govern All-under-Heaven, what cannot change is the Way; what is not simply carried over from one age to the next is ritual. Xia's esteem for wholehearted sincerity and Shang's esteem for simplicity each stood preeminent as the standard of its age. With our Zhou, Kings Wen and Wu possessed enlightened and sagely virtue, while the Duke of Zhou held authority to establish institutions. Thus they looked to Xia and to Shang as models, taking the achievements of those dynasties in ordering the realm as their basis, carefully weighing every detail, and establishing sound laws for their own age. They reduced what was excessive and supplied what was lacking. Building upon the unfolding temper of the times, they carried forward the intentions of the former kings and brought the canons and rites to their fullest realization. Where there was earnestness and sincerity, cultural refinement complemented them. Ranks, forms, regulations, and procedures were supremely detailed and complete, bringing All-under-Heaven to a state of manifest brilliance…

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
也朴而略者有文以飾之道德風俗大順大同
協天下於亨嘉之會也郁郁乎何其盛哉丘也
生值其時會逢其適固不能舍周以他從矣念
典刑之不遠是則是效循循然納於軌物之中
幸謨烈之猶存是訓是行亹亹然式於範圍之
内慮自外於大一統之治法而出入起居將由
之以終身也雖曰夏商之禮能言吾豈棄此以
趨彼乎求無悖於大聖人之作為而動容周旋
皆資之以寡過也即使杞宋之後足徵吾豈襲
===
舊以拂經乎夫贊其文盛者所以表制作之隆
决其從周者所以明憲章之志是可以見夫子
之得統於文武周公而文在於兹矣攷昔帝王
之興罔不制禮以飾政至周而制作始備人事
與氣化交贊者也為下不倍夫子之夙心惟王
盡制又其所嘉尚而尊信焉者而况周禮在魯
乎周公之夢東周之想夫子蓋惓惓焉故曰吾
從周又曰舍魯何適噫周官之法度具在簡編
得其意不泥其迹固可行之萬世而無弊也

punctuated:
也。朴而略者，有文以飾之，道德風俗大順大同，協天下於亨嘉之會也。郁郁乎，何其盛哉！丘也生值其時，會逢其適，固不能舍周以他從矣。念典刑之不遠，是則是效，循循然納於軌物之中；幸謨烈之猶存，是訓是行，亹亹然式於範圍之内。慮自外於大一統之治法，而出入起居將由之以終身也。雖曰夏商之禮能言，吾豈棄此以趨彼乎？求無悖於大聖人之作為，而動容周旋皆資之以寡過也。即使杞宋之後足徵，吾豈襲舊以拂經乎？夫贊其文盛者，所以表制作之隆；决其從周者，所以明憲章之志。是可以見夫子之得統於文武周公，而文在於兹矣。
攷昔帝王之興，罔不制禮以飾政，至周而制作始備，人事與氣化交贊者也。為下不倍，夫子之夙心；惟王盡制，又其所嘉尚而尊信焉者，而况周禮在魯乎？周公之夢，東周之想，夫子蓋惓惓焉。故曰：「吾從周。」又曰：「舍魯何適？」噫！周官之法度具在簡編，得其意，不泥其迹，固可行之萬世而無弊也。
translation_en:
… Where things were plain and unelaborated, cultural refinement adorned them; moral conduct and customs attained great harmony and concord, bringing all under Heaven together in a flourishing age. How richly cultivated, how magnificent it was! I, Qiu [Confucius], was born in this age and have encountered what suits me; certainly I cannot abandon Zhou to follow another dynasty. Mindful that its exemplary standards are not far removed, I take them as my rule and model, proceeding steadily within the bounds of established norms. Fortunate that its plans and achievements still survive, I learn from them and put them into practice, diligently conforming to their compass. Fearing to place myself outside the governing institutions of the great unified realm, I shall follow them throughout my life, in going out and coming in, in rest and activity. Although I can speak of the rites of Xia and Shang, how could I abandon these to pursue those? Seeking never to contravene the work of the great sages, I draw upon these institutions in every gesture and movement to lessen my faults. Even if the descendants of Xia and Shang in Qi and Song could provide sufficient corroboration, how could I adopt the old ways and violate the enduring norms?
To praise the richness of Zhou’s cultural refinement is to reveal the grandeur of its institutional achievements; to declare the resolve to follow Zhou is to make clear the determination to take its institutions as a model. Here we can see that the Master inherited the tradition of Kings Wen and Wu and the Duke of Zhou, and that their culture resided in him.
Examining the rise of emperors and kings in antiquity, we find that all established rites to adorn their government; only under Zhou did these institutions become complete. Human affairs and the transforming forces of nature thus assisted one another. To occupy a subordinate position without disloyalty was the Master’s abiding intention. That the king alone should establish the full system of institutions was likewise a principle he esteemed, revered, and trusted. How much more so when the rites of Zhou survived in Lu! In his dreams of the Duke of Zhou and his thoughts of creating an Eastern Zhou, the Master surely cherished them devotedly. Thus he said, “I follow Zhou,” and again, “If I leave Lu, where shall I go?” Ah! The laws and standards of the Offices of Zhou remain fully preserved in its written text. If one grasps their intent without clinging rigidly to their outward forms, they can indeed be practiced for ten thousand generations without ill effect.

大賢舉爲學之要而歸諸存心，欲人之求仁也。
夫人之弗仁，以心之放也。反而求之，則仁矣。爲學之道，孰有要於此者哉？孟子之意謂夫天下之理，不假於外求；君子之學，莫貴於知要。吾獨慨學之靡要，而仁之日遠也。今夫人之於學也，擴多聞之識而學以聚之，勉勉焉以勵其進；致精義之功而問以辨之，亹亹焉以嚮于成。斯固下學之事也。要之，學問之道，精切而易簡者，豈有他哉？求其放心而已矣。蓋心至微而神者也，虛靈不昧，而感通之妙具焉；出入無時，而存亡
translation_en:
“The way of learning and inquiry is nothing other than seeking one’s strayed mind.”
Zha Guangshu
Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor, comments: “Precise and closely reasoned; it grasps Mencius’s intention in making this statement.”
Associate Examiner Pan, Instructor, comments: “The language and ideas are profound and expansive; the writer evidently has some insight into the learning of the mind.”
Examiner Sun, Right Mentor, comments: “Unhurried and elegant.”
Examiner Guo, Reader-in-Waiting, comments: “Concise and clear.”
The great worthy sets forth the essential point of learning and locates it in preserving the mind, wishing people to seek benevolence.
People fail to be benevolent because they let their minds stray. If they turn back and seek them, they become benevolent. In the way of learning, what could be more essential than this? Mencius’s meaning is this: the principles of all under Heaven need not be sought outside oneself; in the gentleman’s learning, nothing is more valuable than knowing what is essential. I lament only that learning lacks this essential focus and that benevolence grows more distant by the day. Now, in pursuing learning, people broaden the knowledge gained from extensive hearing and study to accumulate it, diligently spurring their progress. They apply themselves to refining their understanding of principles and inquire to distinguish them, tirelessly working toward accomplishment. These are indeed the tasks of learning through ordinary affairs. Yet, in essence, could the way of learning and inquiry, in its precision, directness, ease, and simplicity, be anything else? It is merely to seek one’s strayed mind. The mind is supremely subtle and numinous. Empty, alert, and unobscured, it possesses the wondrous capacity to respond and connect. translation_en:
…and the subtle turning point between its preservation and loss is fleeting. Drawn by encounters with things, the mind sometimes goes astray, racing outward. To return before straying far, one must urgently work at returning properly. Thus one holds fast to and preserves the mind, never forgetting it amid affairs; through purification and reverent vigilance, one makes its spiritual awareness clear, striving to restore its original substance of luminous awareness. One maintains restraint without interruption, whether in private or in public; cleansing the mind and keeping it hidden in secrecy, one strives to regain its true clarity and unity. One restrains its waywardness and preserves its goodness, so that it has a master yet remains open, unshackled by the harm of material desires. One regulates outward conduct to nourish what is within, so that the mind is free of desire and tranquil, undisturbed by selfish impulses to contend and acquire. When the mind is preserved, benevolence is preserved, and the work of learning is complete. Indeed, beyond this one mind there is no further benevolence, and beyond recovering the strayed mind there is no further learning! Otherwise, through obscurity and unrestrained indulgence, the mind strays further each day and benevolence grows ever more remote. Is this not still more deeply lamentable?
Yet, in discussing the way of learning, those dazzled by breadth [?] are indeed diffuse and accomplish nothing, while those absorbed in stillness are likewise lost in obscurity and have nothing firm to rely upon. Both are equally distant from the Way. Why is this? The mind governs our responses to things, and benevolence is the principle inherent in it. This principle certainly need not be sought outside oneself; yet excellence in holding fast to, preserving, and nurturing the mind comes from the effort of learning. Zisi said: “The gentleman honors his moral nature and pursues inquiry and learning.” Is this not the complete achievement of their mutual cultivation? Does Mencius’s statement about recovering the strayed mind not express Zisi’s meaning? If students consider the two together, they can understand the teaching transmitted by Zisi and Mencius.
Book of Changes
“In Return, do we not see the heart of Heaven and Earth?”

Yuan Hongyu

Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor, comments: “Vigorous diction and elevated style: an examination essay on the meaning of the Classics that possesses the spirit of antiquity.”

Associate Examiner Su, School Instructor, comments: “The heart of Heaven and Earth that brings forth living things never ceases. The sage was moved by Return, and therefore spoke of seeing this heart. This composition grasps that meaning and should be recorded as a model.”

Examiner Sun, Right Mentor, comments: “A penetrating explanation of the word ‘heart.’”

Examiner Guo, Reader-in-Waiting, comments: “Highly original, yet governed by proper method.”

Observe the movement of the single yang line, and the heart of the creative process that brings forth living things becomes manifest. For the creative process takes bringing forth living things as its heart. If we observe it in the movement of the single yang line, can we not thereby see its heart? When the Master, in his Commentary on the Judgment of Return, reaches this point, his meaning is this: what transforms and generates the myriad things, enduring without cessation, is the heart of Heaven and Earth; what flows through the four seasons, changing without any fixed form, is the outward trace of the creative process. The heart never alters, but its outward traces shift. As yang wanes in Stripping Away and is exhausted in the Receptive, the heart of Heaven and Earth seems almost to have ceased. Only when this single yang line returns does it draw back the primordial vital force just as that force begins its return: after concealment, it sprouts, initiating the gradual emergence of life. It directs the wondrous efficacy of creation in its silent operation: from closing to opening, it sets in motion the workings of transformation and nurture. What went before has contracted, and what comes now can therefore expand. This expansion is the heart of Heaven and Earth. Within the Great Void, there seems to be something abiding that cannot be thrown into disorder…

translation_en:
… When stillness has reached its end, movement begins anew. This beginning is the heart of Heaven and Earth. Beyond the silent void, there seems to be something governing it that cannot be confounded. Amid contraction and withdrawal into storage, where, ultimately, does this heart reside? After the deep yin has closed and congealed, something remains that cannot be extinguished, and there we encounter it. Amid returning to the root and restoring the mandate of life, where, ultimately, does this heart go? As vital energy first begins to grow, something remains that cannot be obstructed, and there we meet it. At the juncture of completion and origination, life arises spontaneously; the subtle incipience of ease and simplicity is so abundant that one could scoop it up in one’s hands. The true moving impulse of the Limitless and the essential profundities of Supreme Harmony are revealed here. Expanded from this point, it becomes emergence in Zhen, the trigram of Thunder, and the manifestation of benevolence. Its functioning is inexhaustible, yet its heart has already become visible here. Great indeed is Return! Benevolent indeed is the heart of Heaven and Earth! Thus those skilled in observing Heaven and Earth must seek their heart; those skilled in observing their heart must seek it in Return. Ah, how subtle it is!

I have maintained that the heart of Heaven and Earth consists simply in bringing the myriad things to life. Yet things cannot live unless they are shaken, stirred, and made firm. Thus thunder shakes them, wind stirs them, and congealing ice and freezing frost [?] make them firm: all of this serves life. Where, then, is the heart of Heaven and Earth absent? Where can it not be seen? Yet it is said that one must see it in Return. This is because only the sage, whose virtue accords with Heaven and Earth, can apprehend their heart in silence. Those below this level remain bewildered and do not understand it. Might the statement about seeing the heart also be intended to awaken the people, out of concern that they might cling to outward traces and resent Heaven and Earth? Thus encompassing the Way of all under Heaven, opening up an understanding of things, and bringing affairs to completion are what the Book of Changes accomplishes.

“He resembles Heaven and Earth and therefore does not contravene them. His wisdom encompasses the myriad things, and his Way brings aid to all under Heaven; therefore he does not go astray. He acts in diverse directions without drifting away. He delights in Heaven and understands his allotted destiny; therefore he is free from anxiety. He rests content where he dwells and is steadfast in benevolence; therefore he can love.”

What enables the sage to form a triad with Heaven and Earth is simply his embodiment of both wisdom and benevolence. For wisdom and benevolence are the Way of Heaven and Earth and the virtues of human nature. By fully realizing his nature, he forms a triad with Heaven and Earth. Is this not the sage’s consummate achievement? The intent of the Great Commentary is, broadly, that the Book of Changes provides resources for the learning of sages. This is true not only of fathoming principles: one also relies upon it to realize one’s nature fully. Why is this? When Heaven and Earth give birth to human beings, all possess a constant nature. title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
或不達其知不已過乎今也通微之睿周萬物
於無遺而容保之恩濟天下於無外可知也亦
可行也君子以為不過也苟行權矣而正或不
守於仁不已病乎今也識見旁通遷就於一時
之變而機宜妙合不失乎萬世之常雖權也未
嘗流也君子以為猶經也凡知之未深者累於
物未必無憂聖人則樂乎天理而已矣知有天
命而已矣性通於氣之外而遇不足以戕之是
故無憂無憂其知不益深與凡仁之未篤者滯
===
於私未必能愛聖人則隨所處而皆安矣隨所
安而皆仁矣心體乎物之中而迹不足以格之
是故能愛能愛其仁不益篤與夫仁知性也具
之而不憂形之而能愛達之而通事變推之而
濟天下廓之而配天地非天下之至聖其孰能
與於此嗚呼易冒天下之道絪縕相盪動靜相
感浮沉聚散屈伸無非教也故曰陰陽合一存
乎道自夫仁者見之謂之仁知者見之謂之知
而君子之道鮮矣故曰仁知合一存乎聖聖人

或不達，其知不已過乎？今也通微之睿，周萬物於無遺，而容保之恩，濟天下於無外。可知也，亦可行也，君子以為不過也。苟行權矣，而正或不守，於仁不已病乎？今也識見旁通，遷就於一時之變，而機宜妙合，不失乎萬世之常。雖權也，未嘗流也，君子以為猶經也。凡知之未深者，累於物，未必無憂。聖人則樂乎天理而已矣，知有天命而已矣。性通於氣之外，而遇不足以戕之，是故無憂。無憂，其知不益深與？凡仁之未篤者，滯於私，未必能愛。聖人則隨所處而皆安矣，隨所安而皆仁矣。心體乎物之中，而迹不足以格之，是故能愛。能愛，其仁不益篤與？

夫仁知，性也。具之而不憂，形之而能愛，達之而通事變，推之而濟天下，廓之而配天地，非天下之至聖，其孰能與於此？

嗚呼！易冒天下之道，絪縕相盪，動靜相感，浮沉聚散屈伸，無非教也。故曰：「陰陽合一存乎道。」自夫仁者見之謂之仁，知者見之謂之知，而君子之道鮮矣。故曰：「仁知合一存乎聖。」聖人
translation_en:
…should fail to extend that far, would his wisdom not have gone too far? As it is, his sagacity penetrates the subtle and comprehends all things without omission, while his benevolence embraces and protects, bringing aid to all under Heaven without exclusion. What can be known can also be put into practice; the gentleman considers that this does not overstep the bounds. If one exercises discretion but sometimes fails to uphold what is right, would this not already be a defect in benevolence? As it is, his understanding reaches in every direction, adapting to the changes of a particular moment, while his responses accord perfectly with what circumstances require, never departing from the constant principles of all ages. Though he exercises discretion, he never drifts astray; the gentleman considers this equivalent to adhering to the constant norm. Those whose wisdom is not yet deep are burdened by things and cannot necessarily be free from anxiety. The sage simply delights in Heaven’s principle and recognizes Heaven’s mandate. His nature reaches beyond material force, and what befalls him cannot injure it; thus he is without anxiety. In being without anxiety, is his wisdom not all the deeper? Those whose benevolence is not yet steadfast are obstructed by selfishness and cannot necessarily love others. The sage is at peace wherever he finds himself and is benevolent wherever he is at peace. His mind embodies itself within things, and outward circumstances cannot obstruct it; thus he can love others. In being able to love, is his benevolence not all the more steadfast?

Benevolence and wisdom are human nature. Possessing them, he is without anxiety; manifesting them, he can love others; bringing them to full realization, he comprehends changing affairs; extending them, he brings aid to all under Heaven; expanding them, he becomes a counterpart to Heaven and Earth. Who but the most consummate sage under Heaven could attain this?

Ah! The Changes encompasses the Way of all under Heaven. The generative forces intermingle and stir one another; movement and stillness respond to one another. Floating and sinking, gathering and dispersing, contracting and extending—all offer instruction. Thus it is said: “The union of yin and yang lies in the Way.” Yet once the benevolent see it and call it benevolence, and the wise see it and call it wisdom, the Way of the gentleman becomes rare. Thus it is said: “The union of benevolence and wisdom lies in the sage.” The sage…

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
卑職有内外事有大小若是乎其不齊矣然敬
也者所以合崇卑内外大小而一之者也是必
念付托之維艱所以居乎其位者有嚴有翼共
效夫精白之心思凝承之不易所以業乎其官
者無怠無荒各勵其靖共之節蓋今日之事非
予一人之所私也天命之君而君命之臣其功
寔天功也則寅亮之職有不可以不盡者矣亦
非汝諸臣之所私也臣受於君而君受於天其
事皆天事也則欽若之責有不容於他諉者矣
===
夙夜匪懈期於一德以相成凡彌綸参贊之化
莫不承天而時行可也若斯須之不敬是爲褻
天豈予所望於汝諸臣者哉朝夕惟寅期於同
心而共濟凡裁成輔相之道莫不代天以有終
可也若日奏於罔功是爲怠命豈諸臣所以副
予之望者哉夫勵之以敬而遡之於天帝舜所
以訓迪乎羣臣者詞不繁而意獨至矣抑論舜
曰惟時亮天功既以天而命其臣皐陶陳謨曰
天工人其代之復以天而贊其君君臣交相儆

punctuated:
卑，職有内外，事有大小，若是乎其不齊矣！然敬也者，所以合崇卑内外大小而一之者也。是必念付托之維艱，所以居乎其位者，有嚴有翼，共效夫精白之心；思凝承之不易，所以業乎其官者，無怠無荒，各勵其靖共之節。蓋今日之事，非予一人之所私也。天命之君，而君命之臣，其功寔天功也，則寅亮之職，有不可以不盡者矣。亦非汝諸臣之所私也。臣受於君，而君受於天，其事皆天事也，則欽若之責，有不容於他諉者矣。夙夜匪懈，期於一德以相成，凡彌綸参贊之化，莫不承天而時行可也。若斯須之不敬，是爲褻天，豈予所望於汝諸臣者哉？朝夕惟寅，期於同心而共濟，凡裁成輔相之道，莫不代天以有終可也。若日奏於罔功，是爲怠命，豈諸臣所以副予之望者哉？

夫勵之以敬，而遡之於天，帝舜所以訓迪乎羣臣者，詞不繁而意獨至矣。抑論舜曰：「惟時亮天功。」既以天而命其臣，皐陶陳謨曰：「天工人其代之。」復以天而贊其君。君臣交相儆
translation_en:
…low; offices have responsibilities within and without; affairs are great and small. How varied they are! Yet reverence brings together high and low, inner and outer, great and small, and unites them. You must reflect on the difficulty of the trust committed to you: in occupying your positions, be solemn and circumspect, together offering hearts of pure sincerity. Consider how difficult it is to bear this weighty charge: in carrying out your offices, be neither idle nor negligent, each cultivating the integrity of devoted, respectful service. For the affairs of this day are not my private concern alone. Heaven appoints the ruler, and the ruler appoints his ministers. Their accomplishments are truly Heaven’s accomplishments; thus the duty of reverently assisting cannot be left unfulfilled. Nor are these affairs the private concern of you ministers. Ministers receive their charge from the ruler, and the ruler receives his from Heaven. Their affairs are all Heaven’s affairs; thus the responsibility of reverent compliance cannot be shifted to others.

Be unremitting morning and night, aspiring to complete one another’s efforts through unity in virtue. In all your work of comprehensively ordering and assisting the transforming processes, act in accordance with Heaven and at the proper time. Even a moment’s irreverence would be an affront to Heaven. Could that be what I expect of you ministers? Be reverent morning and evening, aspiring to work together with one heart. In all your ways of shaping, completing, and assisting, act on Heaven’s behalf and carry matters through to completion. If day after day you achieve nothing, this is to neglect your charge. Could this be how you ministers fulfill my hopes?

Urging them to reverence and tracing its source to Heaven: thus did Emperor Shun instruct and guide his ministers. His words were few, yet their meaning was supremely profound. Moreover, consider Shun’s words: “Reverently assist in Heaven’s accomplishments.” He thereby invoked Heaven in charging his ministers. Gao Yao, presenting his counsels, said: “Heaven’s work is for men to perform on its behalf.” He in turn invoked Heaven in assisting his ruler. Ruler and ministers admonished one another…

translation_en:
…admonished one another, encouraging the resolve to accomplish difficult tasks and fully discharge the duty of serving Heaven. Was this not why government under the house of Yu flourished? A ruler serves Heaven as he serves his father; a minister serves his ruler as he serves Heaven. The principle is the same. Ah! This can serve as a mirror for those who seek good government.
“Heaven bestowed its full protection and mandate; thus Shang was filled with men of the great clans and royal servants, all of whom upheld virtue. It showed enlightened concern for the lesser ministers and sheltered the lords of the hou and dian domains—how much more those who all hastened to serve.”
Wang Yilin
Associate Examiner Zhang, Instructor, comments: “Both expression and reasoning are fully accomplished. Essays on the Book of Documents of this quality are very rare.”
Associate Examiner Chen, Director of Studies, comments: “Concise yet elegant, gentle yet incisive: truly an outstanding work. Accept it.”
Examiner Sun, Right Mentor, comments: “Words that penetrate principle.”
Examiner Guo, Reader-in-Waiting, comments: “The expression and meaning are clear and vivid.”
The great minister explains how Shang received Heaven’s abundant favor and enjoyed the assistance of many worthy men. The flourishing or decline of a state depends upon worthy talent. Could it have been mere chance that Shang received Heaven’s favor and obtained the assistance of so many worthy men? When the Duke of Zhou urged the Duke of Shao to remain in office, he touched upon this point, as though saying: “Good government in the world always depends upon worthy men, and the birth of worthy men ultimately has its source in Heaven. Everyone knows that Shang had many worthy men; yet who understands Heaven’s favor toward Shang? Heaven’s mandate has no fixed recipient: it is granted only to virtue. title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
純一而不雜匪諶之妙克敬惟親也而申命用
休以寵綏乎商者孔固而無貳由是篤生衆哲
而思皇之士萃于王國庶明收勵翼之功也降
此才賢而藹吉之人列于庶位家國靡空虛之
患也商不於是而實乎是故以言乎其內也由
百官著姓下逮王官之微位固有尊卑矣罔不
秉持其德而懷忠貞之誠明致其恤而篤靖共
之節其在內也不既有人矣乎以言乎其外也
自凡百執事上至屏侯甸之重職固有小大矣
===
矧皆駿奔王命而宣力之惟勤趨走王事而鞠
瘁之匪懈其在外也不既有人矣乎是皆商實
之徵純佑之命也而諸臣輔德之功曷可少哉
君奭其求匹美于商臣可也豈可以盛滿為懼
而果於求去也耶抑觀周公稱商受天之命得
賢之益所以留召公者意誠委曲而切至矣夫
天之生賢實畀之輔世之責而不容以自逸賢
之去就則又有時中之道而不可苟者召公之
欲老進退之義守道之常也周公之勉留休戚

translation_en:
…was pure and undivided. The subtle working of Heaven, which cannot be relied upon, is to favor those capable of reverence; thus its renewed mandate of blessing, by which it favored and secured Shang, was exceedingly firm and unwavering. Consequently, it brought forth many wise men, and splendid gentlemen gathered in the royal realm: men of manifold discernment achieved the work of diligent assistance. It sent down these talented and worthy men, and the multitude of good men occupied the various offices, so that the ruling house and state suffered no lack of personnel. Was not Shang thereby abundantly provided for?

Thus, speaking of those within the court, from the prominent lineages among the hundred officials down to the humblest royal officers, their ranks certainly differed in dignity. Yet all upheld their virtue and cherished sincere loyalty and constancy; all clearly gave expression to their solicitude and steadfastly maintained devoted, respectful service. Was there not already an abundance of capable men within? Speaking of those outside the court, from the many officers charged with affairs up to the weighty posts of the regional lords who served as its protective screen, their responsibilities certainly differed in magnitude. Yet all hastened to obey the king’s commands and diligently exerted their strength, hurried about the king’s affairs and tirelessly devoted themselves to exhaustion. Was there not already an abundance of capable men outside? These were all proofs of Shang’s abundance and of Heaven’s mandate of unqualified protection. How, then, could the ministers’ achievement in assisting royal virtue be considered slight?

“Lord Shi, you should seek to equal the excellence of Shang’s ministers. How could you fear the fullness of prosperity and therefore resolve to seek retirement?” Consider, moreover, how the Duke of Zhou invoked Shang’s receipt of Heaven’s mandate and the benefits of obtaining worthy men in order to persuade the Duke of Shao to remain. His intention was indeed delicately expressed, yet earnest and deeply felt. When Heaven brings forth worthy men, it truly entrusts them with responsibility for assisting the world and does not permit them to indulge in ease. Yet in deciding whether to withdraw or serve, worthy men must also follow the way of acting appropriately to the time; they cannot act carelessly. The Duke of Shao’s wish to retire exemplified the righteousness governing advancement and withdrawal, and the constant principle of keeping to the Way. The Duke of Zhou’s urging him to remain, in prosperity and adversity …

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
七而飼養之如一是其所性之恒而得夫均一
之端者矣物且然况淑人君子乎蘊純粹之懿
而行臻夫可欲備美大之實而德底于有成見
于一身者雖不同也而淑慎之止咸納于範圍
可觀可度又斬其一致乎動乎四體者雖不一
也而柔嘉之則允協夫中正中規中矩始終其
不渝乎其儀之一如此豈致飾于貌而弗由干
衷者耶以言乎其心也端凝靜之體而收斂維
至主宰之中存專確而不雜也秉堅厲之操而
===
貞固有恒神明之內蘊純一而不貳也有如物
之固結而不可解焉其心之純如此謂非儀一
之本哉是知儀一則表肅心純則志貞內外交
養君子之德其至矣乎大抵心者萬物之原治
亂之本也唐虞三代茂矣後世秉心塞淵者振
衰頹之業思無邪者獲富庶之效皆此道也曹
俗玩細娛而忘遠圖鳲鳩詩人歌淑人焉其悼
世變而植民表之志耶有民位之寄者宜知所
鑒矣

七，而飼養之如一，是其所性之恒，而得夫均一之端者矣。物且然，况淑人君子乎？蘊純粹之懿，而行臻夫可欲；備美大之實，而德底于有成。見于一身者雖不同也，而淑慎之止咸納于範圍，可觀可度，又斬其一致乎？動乎四體者雖不一也，而柔嘉之則允協夫中正，中規中矩，始終其不渝乎？其儀之一如此，豈致飾于貌而弗由干衷者耶？以言乎其心也，端凝靜之體，而收斂維至，主宰之中存專確而不雜也；秉堅厲之操，而貞固有恒，神明之內蘊純一而不貳也。有如物之固結而不可解焉。其心之純如此，謂非儀一之本哉？是知儀一則表肅，心純則志貞，內外交養，君子之德其至矣乎！

大抵心者，萬物之原，治亂之本也。唐虞三代茂矣，後世秉心塞淵者振衰頹之業，思無邪者獲富庶之效，皆此道也。曹俗玩細娛而忘遠圖，鳲鳩詩人歌淑人焉，其悼世變而植民表之志耶？有民位之寄者宜知所鑒矣。
translation_en:
…seven, yet it feeds and nurtures them all alike. This is the constancy of its inherent nature, displaying the beginnings of evenhandedness and singleness of purpose. If even a creature is like this, how much more so a good and noble man! He harbors the excellence of unalloyed purity, and his conduct attains what is worthy of desire; he possesses the substance of beauty and greatness, and his virtue reaches fulfillment. Although the qualities manifested in his person differ, his good and careful deportment falls entirely within proper bounds. Worthy of observation and emulation, does it not also display a clear unity [?]? Although the movements of his four limbs vary, their gentle and admirable standards accord truly with centrality and correctness. Conforming to compass and square, do they not remain unchanged from beginning to end? Such is the consistency of his bearing: could it be an embellishment of outward appearance that does not proceed from within [?]? As for his heart, he maintains a composed and tranquil disposition, gathering himself inward with the utmost care; within this governing center there abides a focused firmness, free of admixture. He holds to a steadfast and rigorous resolve, remaining constant in rectitude; within his spiritual awareness lies a purity and singleness that admits no division. It is like something firmly bound together that cannot be undone. Such is the purity of his heart: can one say that it is not the foundation of his consistent bearing? Thus we know that when bearing is consistent, outward demeanor is reverent; when the heart is pure, purpose is steadfast. With inner and outer mutually nourishing each other, has not the noble man's virtue reached its highest perfection?

In general, the heart is the source of all things and the foundation of order and disorder. Under Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties, this flourished. In later ages, those whose hearts were sincere and profound revived declining undertakings, while those whose thoughts were without perversity achieved prosperity and abundance. All followed this Way. The people of Cao, in their customs, indulged in petty amusements and forgot far-reaching plans. The poet of “The Cuckoo” therefore sang of the good man: was his intention to lament the changes of his age and establish an exemplar for the people? Those entrusted with positions over the people should know what lesson to draw from this.

夫德，治之本也。况文德之純，而所以綱紀四方者，不已至耶？詩人發之詠歌，見儀刑之有在也。豈不曰：聖之至者，其心愈下；而德之盛者，其化必神。人見文王得人而造周矣，是豈偶然之故哉？維我文王，至誠無息，緝熈體維天之命，純亦不已；小心纘聖敬之躋。雖曰性與天合，非有所勉也，而憂勤惕厲之心，日昃不遑者，其天行之健矣乎！雖曰優入聖域，無待於爲也，而兢業彊勉之志，維日不足者，其恒久之貞矣乎！勉勉我
translation_en:
“Diligent, diligent is our king, ordering and regulating the four quarters.”
Zha Guangshu
Associate Examiner Yang, an Education Instructor, comments: “Precise in expression and reasoning, it skillfully brings out the depths of King Wen’s virtue. Accept it.”
Associate Examiner Pan, an Education Instructor, comments: “Pure and elegant, graceful yet disciplined: it can serve as a standard for correcting frivolous ornamentation.”
Examiner Sun, Right Rectifier of the Heir Apparent, comments: “It explains the Poetry well.”
Examiner Guo, a Hanlin Reader-in-waiting, comments: “Explaining ‘diligent, diligent’ through the word ‘pure’ is quite right.”
The poet sings of the sage’s unifying rule through pure virtue, expressing admiration and yearning to the utmost.
Virtue is the foundation of government. How much more so the purity of King Wen’s virtue: was not the means by which he ordered and regulated the four quarters already perfect? The poet gives expression to this in song, showing where the model to be emulated lies. Does this not mean that the more perfect a sage is, the humbler his heart, and the more abundant his virtue, the more wondrous his transforming influence must be? People see that King Wen won men’s allegiance and established Zhou. Could this have happened by chance? Our King Wen’s utmost sincerity never ceased. Through sustained illumination, he embodied Heaven’s mandate, whose purity likewise never ceases; with a cautious heart, he continued the ascent of sagely reverence. Although his nature accorded with Heaven and required no exertion, his anxious, diligent, vigilant heart allowed him no leisure even when the sun declined: was this not the vigor of Heaven’s movement? Although he entered the realm of sagehood with ease, without depending on deliberate effort, his resolve to remain watchful and strive tirelessly made each day seem insufficient: was this not enduring constancy? title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
王所以達之治理者何如耶志意之孚足以繫
方國之心精神之運足以周天下之故綱焉斯
張範圍之而不過也四方之廣合其渙而萃其
離者一誠冒之而無外矣紀焉斯理曲成之而
不遺也億兆之衆聯其異而比其同者一心用
之而有餘矣玆文德之純而人心自不能外也
使有間焉則不足以為德而何綱紀之足云噫
此文王之所以為文而周之所以為周也聖德
神化庸非后王之矩乎抑文王之聖至矣詩人
===
稱述之者不過曰亹亹緝熈翼翼勉勉云爾豈
生知安行之聖猶待於矜飭懋進也耶噫此善
發聖人之蘊者也亹緝翼勉固文王所以聖也
若但要其所造之域而不本其存主之心則豈
善言聖德者哉孟子有言文王視民如傷望道
而未之見其亦詩人之旨乎周之德其可謂至
德也已矣
春秋
秋八月壬午大閱〔桓公六年〕

春秋
秋，八月，壬午，大閱。〔桓公六年〕
translation_en:
…our king—how did he extend this into orderly government? The sincerity of his intentions sufficed to bind the hearts of the regional states; the workings of his spirit sufficed to encompass all the affairs of the world. He spread the main cords of government, enclosing all within their bounds without overstepping what was proper. Across the vastness of the four quarters, he united the scattered and gathered the separated: his single sincerity embraced everything, leaving nothing outside. He set the lesser cords in order, bringing each thing to fulfillment according to its particular circumstances and neglecting none. Among the countless multitudes, he linked those who differed and brought together those who were alike: the application of his single mind was more than sufficient. Such was the purity of King Wen’s virtue that people’s hearts could not help but be drawn within it. Had there been any interruption in it, it would not have qualified as virtue; what, then, would there have been to say of the ordering cords of government? Ah! This is what made King Wen worthy of the name Wen, and what made Zhou what it was. Were his sagely virtue and wondrous transforming influence not a standard for later kings?

Yet King Wen’s sagehood was of the highest order, while the poets, in praising him, said no more than that he was untiring, continuously bright, reverently attentive, and unremitting in effort. Could a sage who possessed knowledge from birth and practiced the Way with natural ease still have needed vigilant self-discipline and strenuous advancement? Ah! These words aptly disclose what lay within the sage. His tirelessness, continuous cultivation, reverent attentiveness, and unremitting effort were precisely what made King Wen a sage. If one considered only the realm he attained, without tracing it to the mind he preserved and made his guiding authority, how could one speak well of sagely virtue? Mengzi said: “King Wen looked upon the people as though they were injured, and gazed toward the Way as though he had not yet seen it.” Was this not also what the poets meant? The virtue of Zhou may indeed be called the highest virtue.

Spring and Autumn Annals
In autumn, in the eighth month, on the renwu day, a grand military review was held. 〔Sixth year of Duke Huan.〕

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
錢復初
同考試官學正吳批重時嚴分詞義凛
然且達於經國之旨是用錄出
考試官右中允孫批有斷制
考試官侍讀郭批明整
春秋於望國講武而譏其時制之失示經國之
道也蓋經國之道存乎豫也望國講武而時制
皆失焉春秋譏之其以是哉且克詰戎兵先王
之訓也用戒戎作侯國之度也魯之大閱蓋亦
===
祗若先王之訓虔修列侯之度耳春秋譏之者
何夫君子之舉事有時焉以酌緩急之序逆則
厲民有制焉以辨上下之等紊則踰禮是故先
王之治寓軍政于四時之田纘武功于農務之
隙以順時也核軍實于衆寡之數别軍容于旂
鼓之辨以明制也魯也懼鄭忽之訴畏齊兵之
加乃當秋月而簡車徒以侯邦而用大閱雖曰
用戒不虞難以常法拘也不思妨務病農使稼
穡有汙萊之嘆重於用民者肯如是乎雖曰利

錢復初

考試官右中允孫批：有斷制。

春秋於望國講武，而譏其時制之失，示經國之道也。蓋經國之道存乎豫也。望國講武而時制皆失焉，春秋譏之，其以是哉？且克詰戎兵，先王之訓也；用戒戎作，侯國之度也。魯之大閱，蓋亦祗若先王之訓，虔修列侯之度耳。春秋譏之者何？夫君子之舉事，有時焉，以酌緩急之序，逆則厲民；有制焉，以辨上下之等，紊則踰禮。是故先王之治，寓軍政于四時之田，纘武功于農務之隙，以順時也；核軍實于衆寡之數，别軍容于旂鼓之辨，以明制也。魯也，懼鄭忽之訴，畏齊兵之加，乃當秋月而簡車徒，以侯邦而用大閱。雖曰用戒不虞，難以常法拘也，不思妨務病農，使稼穡有汙萊之嘆，重於用民者肯如是乎？雖曰利

Qian Fuchu

Associate Examiner Wu, School Instructor, comments: “He stresses proper timing and strictly observes distinctions of rank. His language and meaning are imposing, and he also comprehends the purport of governing a state. For these reasons, this answer has been selected for inclusion.”
Examiner Sun, Right Mentor, comments: “It displays decisive judgment.”
Examiner Guo, Reader-in-Waiting, comments: “Clear and orderly.”

In recording military exercises in a prominent state, the Spring and Autumn Annals censures failures in their timing and prescribed form, thereby revealing the way to govern a state. For the way to govern a state lies in preparedness. When a prominent state conducts military exercises yet errs in both timing and prescribed form, is this not why the Spring and Autumn Annals censures it? Moreover, keeping military forces in good order was an injunction of the former kings; taking precautions against warfare was a rule for the feudal states. Lu’s grand military review was presumably no more than a reverent observance of the former kings’ injunction and a conscientious fulfillment of the rules for the feudal lords. Why, then, does the Spring and Autumn Annals censure it?

When the gentleman undertakes an affair, there is a proper time, by which he weighs the relative urgency of tasks; to go against it is to harm the people. There are prescribed forms, by which he distinguishes the ranks of superior and subordinate; to disorder them is to transgress ritual propriety. Thus, in their governance, the former kings incorporated military administration into the seasonal hunts and carried on martial achievements during intervals in agricultural work, thereby following the seasons. They inspected military resources according to the numbers of troops and distinguished military displays through differences in flags and drums, thereby making the prescribed forms clear.

Lu, fearing the complaint of Hu of Zheng and an attack by Qi’s forces, inspected its chariots and infantry in an autumn month and, though merely a feudal state, employed a grand military review. One might say that, in guarding against unforeseen events, it was difficult to be bound by ordinary rules. Yet this disregarded the disruption of work and the distress inflicted on farmers, causing lamentation that cultivated fields had become waterlogged or overgrown. Would someone who took seriously the employment of the people’s labor willingly act thus? One might say that it was advantageous …

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
用禦寇難以舊制泥也不思侵上敗度使行伍
易紀律之常堅於秉禮者固如斯乎矧善爲國
者非外侮之患而惟內治之修四時之田其務
周也何至倉卒之舉而違時以動衆耶非禍變
之虞而恃防杜之術千乘之具其飭豫也何至
張皇之甚而踰禮以作事耶觀此則魯桓之失
不可掩而聖人重農嚴分之戒經國豫事之訓
不亦著明也哉抑論桓之爲國固無足言矣魯
能秉禮以周班而次鄭君子猶有取焉以其不
===
失先王之典也忽之怒齊之伐于魯何咎乎使
魯能充其類經國奠民咸取則於周禮其庶幾
爲東周乎惜也知以禮處鄭而不知以禮自處
馴致後世公室弱而私家强君子於此不能不
爲之深慨也
夏齊人伐我北鄙〔僖公二十有六年〕夏公
會齊侯于夾谷公至自夾谷〔定公十年〕
劉璞
同考試官學正吳 批 義悉而詞精末重

用禦寇，難以舊制泥也，不思侵上敗度，使行伍易紀律之常，堅於秉禮者固如斯乎？矧善爲國者，非外侮之患，而惟內治之修。四時之田，其務周也，何至倉卒之舉而違時以動衆耶？非禍變之虞，而恃防杜之術。千乘之具，其飭豫也，何至張皇之甚而踰禮以作事耶？觀此，則魯桓之失不可掩，而聖人重農嚴分之戒、經國豫事之訓，不亦著明也哉？抑論桓之爲國，固無足言矣。魯能秉禮，以周班而次鄭，君子猶有取焉，以其不失先王之典也。忽之怒、齊之伐，于魯何咎乎？使魯能充其類，經國奠民，咸取則於周禮，其庶幾爲東周乎？惜也，知以禮處鄭，而不知以禮自處，馴致後世公室弱而私家强，君子於此不能不爲之深慨也。
夏，齊人伐我北鄙。〔僖公二十有六年〕夏，公會齊侯于夾谷。公至自夾谷。〔定公十年〕

translation_en:
…useful for repelling invaders, and thus not to be constrained by old institutions, they fail to consider that this encroaches upon the authority of superiors and undermines established rules, causing the ranks to depart from their customary discipline. Would someone steadfast in observing ritual propriety really act thus? Moreover, those skilled in governing a state concern themselves with cultivating internal order, rather than worrying about foreign aggression. The seasonal hunts provide comprehensive preparation: why resort to a hasty undertaking, mobilizing the people at an improper season? They rely on measures of prevention rather than fearing calamities and upheavals. Equipment for a thousand chariots is put in order beforehand: why become so alarmed as to undertake actions that exceed ritual bounds? Viewed in this light, Duke Huan of Lu’s fault cannot be concealed. Are not the Sage’s admonitions to value agriculture and maintain strict distinctions of rank, and his teachings on governing a state and preparing for contingencies, clearly manifest?
Yet there is little worth saying about Huan’s government. When Lu observed ritual propriety and took its place after Zheng according to the Zhou order of precedence, the gentleman still found something to commend, since Lu had not abandoned the institutions of the former kings. What fault lay with Lu in Hu of Zheng’s anger or Qi’s attack? Had Lu extended this principle to like matters, taking the rites of Zhou as its model in governing the state and bringing security to the people, might it not nearly have become an eastern Zhou? Alas, it knew how to treat Zheng according to ritual propriety, but not how to conduct itself accordingly. Gradually this led, in later generations, to the weakening of the ducal house and the strengthening of private lineages. The gentleman cannot but lament this deeply.
“In summer, the men of Qi attacked our northern borderlands.” 〔Twenty-sixth year of Duke Xi〕 “In summer, the duke met the Marquis of Qi at Jiagu. The duke returned from Jiagu.” 〔Tenth year of Duke Ding〕
Liu Pu

text:
任賢尤有見
考試官右中允孫批〔得謹嚴體〕
考試官侍讀郭批〔以辭禮立說有關鎖〕
觀聖賢之卻敵有授辭以諭之者有秉禮以服
之者此展禽退北鄙之師仲尼相夾谷之會而
見辭與禮之效大也為國者其可忽諸昔齊之
孝公憤僖黨衛伐魯北鄙時則室如縣罄野無
青草魯蓋恐恐乎危矣不有君子其何能國幸
而有賢如展子者為之謀焉為犒師之辭授于
===
展喜是故夾輔勞賜之盟用昭先王之命棄命
廢職之諭諷其嗣世之愆義正詞嚴雖驕悍如
齊能不繹思而悔禍耶卒之班師以還使魯境
免於侵暴之慘者展子片言之力也不賢而能
之乎君子曰辭之不可以已也其謂是與及齊
之景公要我魯侯會于夾谷時則犁彌獻讒萊
人肆侮定蓋岌岌乎殆矣不有哲人其曷能免
幸而有聖如孔子者寔相會事焉歷階之對斥
乎萊人是故裔夷華夏之辨正其干偪之奸神

之景公要我魯侯會于夾谷時則犁彌獻譏萊
人肆侮定蓋岌岌乎殆矣不有哲人其曷能免
幸而有聖如孔子者寔相會事焉歷階之對斥

…employing the worthy: this is particularly perceptive.
Examiner Sun, Right Mentor, comments: 〔Achieves a careful and rigorous style.〕
Examiner Guo, Reader-in-waiting, comments: 〔Builds the argument around persuasive speech and ritual propriety, with closely connected reasoning.〕
When we observe how sages and worthy men repelled enemies, some supplied speeches to admonish them, while others upheld ritual propriety to bring them into submission. Zhan Qin’s turning back the army from the northern border and Zhongni’s assisting at the meeting at Jiagu demonstrate the great efficacy of speech and ritual propriety. Can those who govern states neglect these?
In former times, Duke Xiao of Qi, angered that Duke Xi had sided with Wei, attacked Lu’s northern border. At the time, houses were as empty as suspended chime stones, and there was no green grass in the fields. Lu was indeed fearful and in peril. Without a man of noble character, how could it maintain itself as a state? Fortunately, a worthy man such as Master Zhan devised a plan for it. He composed a speech to accompany provisions offered to the invading army and gave it to Zhan Xi. Thus, by invoking the covenant concerning joint support for the royal house and rewards for meritorious service, he made manifest the former king’s command; by admonishing them against abandoning that command and neglecting their duties, he indirectly reproached the transgression of their hereditary successor. His principles were correct and his words stern. Even a state as arrogant and fierce as Qi—could it fail to reflect and regret the harm it was causing? That its army ultimately withdrew and returned home, sparing Lu’s territory the misery of invasion and violence, was due to the power of Master Zhan’s few words. Could someone without worthiness have accomplished this? The gentleman says, “Persuasive speech cannot be dispensed with.” Does this not refer to such a case?
Later, Duke Jing of Qi invited our lord of Lu to meet at Jiagu. At that time, Li Mi offered slanderous counsel, and the men of Lai behaved with insolent contempt. Duke Ding was indeed in imminent danger. Without a wise man, how could he have escaped? Fortunately, a sage such as Confucius was actually assisting with the proceedings of the meeting. Ascending the steps, he spoke out and rebuked the men of Lai. Thus, by distinguishing between the outlying barbarians and the civilized central states, he condemned their treacherous aggression and intimidation; the spirits…

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
人德義之常動其愆失之悔理直氣壯雖强暴
如景能不感悟而服義耶卒之謝過以質使魯
君免於劫制之辱者孔子俄頃之助也非聖人
而能若是乎君子曰禮之可以爲國也不其然
與是知辭足以諭敵則命之爲也不可苟禮足
以服敵則禮之執也不可忽若乃不信仁賢而
使國空虛謂非爲國之大患哉大抵仁賢者邦
國之衛也用舍者盛衰之幾也春秋之時鄭以
蕞爾之國而任子産諸賢猶能弘禮修命交睦
===
諸侯爭承毁垣申義强晋況魯國之大而有展
禽之賢孔子之聖乎惜乎魯君罔知任用使柳
下阨于三黜夾谷僅于一試噫此魯之所以終
於不競也與

百物不失節故祀天祭地明則有禮樂
幽則有鬼神
胡應徵

人德義之常，動其愆失之悔。理直氣壯，雖强暴如景，能不感悟而服義耶？卒之謝過以質，使魯君免於劫制之辱者，孔子俄頃之助也。非聖人而能若是乎？君子曰：「禮之可以爲國也。」不其然與？是知辭足以諭敵，則命之爲也不可苟；禮足以服敵，則禮之執也不可忽。若乃不信仁賢，而使國空虛，謂非爲國之大患哉？大抵仁賢者，邦國之衛也；用舍者，盛衰之幾也。春秋之時，鄭以蕞爾之國，而任子産諸賢，猶能弘禮修命，交睦諸侯，爭承毁垣，申義强晋。況魯國之大，而有展禽之賢、孔子之聖乎？惜乎魯君罔知任用，使柳下阨于三黜，夾谷僅于一試。噫！此魯之所以終於不競也與！

禮記

大樂與天地同和，大禮與天地同節。和故百物不失，節故祀天祭地。明則有禮樂，幽則有鬼神。

胡應徵
translation_en:
…the enduring norms of virtue and righteousness shared by spirits and men stirred his remorse for his transgressions. With right on his side and confidence in his words, could even someone as violent and overbearing as Duke Jing fail to awaken to the truth and submit to righteousness? That the duke finally apologized and gave pledges, allowing the ruler of Lu to escape the humiliation of coercion, was due to the assistance Confucius rendered in that brief moment. Could anyone but a sage have accomplished this? The gentleman says, “Ritual can indeed be used to govern a state.” Is this not so?

Thus we know that, since words suffice to bring an adversary to understanding, the drafting of diplomatic communications must not be careless; since ritual suffices to secure an adversary’s submission, its observance must not be neglected. If a ruler fails to trust the humane and worthy, leaving his state bereft of capable men, can this be called anything other than a grave danger to its governance? In general, humane and worthy men are the defenses of a state; whether they are employed or set aside is the pivot of flourishing and decline. During the Spring and Autumn period, Zheng, though a tiny state, employed Zichan and other worthy men. It could therefore promote ritual, refine its diplomatic communications, maintain harmonious relations with the other lords, contest the matter of demolishing walls [?], and uphold righteousness before mighty Jin. How much more could the great state of Lu have accomplished, possessing a man as worthy as Zhan Qin and a sage like Confucius! Alas, the ruler of Lu did not know how to employ them: Liuxia—that is, Zhan Qin—suffered the adversity of three dismissals, while Confucius was given only a single opportunity at Jiagu. Ah! Was this not why Lu ultimately remained weak?

Record of Rites

“Great music shares the harmony of Heaven and Earth; great ritual shares their ordered distinctions. Through harmony, the myriad things retain their proper places; through ordered distinctions, sacrifices are offered to Heaven and Earth. In the visible realm there are ritual and music; in the hidden realm there are ghosts and spirits.”

Hu Yingzheng

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官學正黃批嚴整渾融非深於
禮樂者不能道
考試官右中允孫批和而莊
考試官侍讀郭批理明詞鬯
觀禮樂有合乎造化可見其一理也蓋禮樂與
造化相流通者也名雖以迹而異而其理豈有
不一也哉且禮者聖人之所制樂者聖人之所
作也制作出於聖人若與天地不相關矣然其
始也明於天地而興禮樂則其成功寧無脗合
===
者乎何則聖人之大樂情不可變至和也天地
有自然之和而樂寔與之同其和焉聖人之大
禮理不可易至節也天地有自然之節而禮寔
與之同其節焉夫惟其和也故能順氣而敦和
凡物之親上者若其性凡物之親下者遂其生
而天地之化不過矣大樂之作不有以贊之耶
夫惟其節也故能達數而别宜祀圓丘所以報
乎天祭方澤所以報乎地而天地之德已昭矣
大禮之制不有以贊之耶由是觀之禮樂鬼神

觀禮樂有合乎造化，可見其一理也。蓋禮樂與造化相流通者也，名雖以迹而異，而其理豈有不一也哉？且禮者，聖人之所制；樂者，聖人之所作也。制作出於聖人，若與天地不相關矣。然其始也，明於天地而興禮樂，則其成功寧無脗合者乎？何則？聖人之大樂，情不可變，至和也。天地有自然之和，而樂寔與之同其和焉。聖人之大禮，理不可易，至節也。天地有自然之節，而禮寔與之同其節焉。夫惟其和也，故能順氣而敦和。凡物之親上者若其性，凡物之親下者遂其生，而天地之化不過矣。大樂之作，不有以贊之耶？夫惟其節也，故能達數而别宜。祀圓丘，所以報乎天；祭方澤，所以報乎地，而天地之德已昭矣。大禮之制，不有以贊之耶？由是觀之，禮樂鬼神
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Huang, an Instructor, comments: “Rigorous and orderly, thoroughly integrated: only someone deeply versed in rites and music could express this.”
Examiner Sun, Right Rectifier of the Heir Apparent, comments: “Harmonious yet dignified.”
Examiner Guo, a Reader-in-Waiting, comments: “Clear in principle and fluent in expression.”
Observing how rites and music accord with the transformations of nature, we can see that they share a single principle. Rites and music interpenetrate the workings of nature. Although their names differ according to their outward manifestations, how could their underlying principle fail to be one? Rites are what the sage institutes; music is what the sage creates. Since their institution and creation proceed from the sage, they might seem unrelated to Heaven and Earth. Yet at the outset he understands Heaven and Earth and thereby brings forth rites and music. Could their completed achievement then fail to accord with Heaven and Earth?
Why is this so? The sage’s great music, whose essential character cannot change, is consummate harmony. Heaven and Earth possess a natural harmony, and music truly shares that harmony. The sage’s great rites, whose principle cannot be altered, are consummate measure. Heaven and Earth possess a natural measure, and rites truly share that measure. Precisely because of this harmony, music can guide vital energies along their proper course and deepen concord. All things drawn upward follow their nature; all things drawn downward fulfill their life, and the transformations of Heaven and Earth do not exceed their proper bounds. Does not the creation of great music help bring this about?
Precisely because of this measure, rites can give full expression to prescribed observances and distinguish what is fitting. Sacrifice at the Round Mound repays Heaven; sacrifice at the Square Pool repays Earth. Thus the beneficent powers of Heaven and Earth are made manifest. Does not the institution of great rites help bring this about? Viewed in this light, rites and music, ghosts and spirits…

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
非判然為二物者也自明而言則謂之禮樂禮
之制也以飾天下之治樂之作也以宣天下之
功蓋闡無於有見聖人之成能焉耳自幽而言
則謂之鬼神陰之屈也凝其氣以為收斂陽之
伸也舒其氣以為發生蓋藏有於無妙造化之
功用焉耳其實禮樂也鬼神也一理也是故樂
之敦和者率神而從天禮之别宜者居鬼而從
地豈可以差殊觀也哉吁天人合其和節事理
通於幽明知乎此則可與同民心而出治道矣
===
嘗攷樂由天作禮以地制天地者禮樂之本也
聖王馭世其始也法天地以為禮樂其終也以
禮樂而贊天地要之與道為一故形之制作無
有乎弗合後世拘拘器數而不求端於天地豈
先王之意哉故曰不聞性與天道而能制禮作
樂者末矣
禮之先幣帛也欲民之先事而後祿也
陳思武
同考試官學正黃 批 雅健精醇記義之
