非判然為二物者也。自明而言，則謂之禮樂。禮之制也，以飾天下之治；樂之作也，以宣天下之功。蓋闡無於有，見聖人之成能焉耳。自幽而言，則謂之鬼神。陰之屈也，凝其氣以為收斂；陽之伸也，舒其氣以為發生。蓋藏有於無，妙造化之功用焉耳。其實禮樂也，鬼神也，一理也。是故樂之敦和者，率神而從天；禮之别宜者，居鬼而從地。豈可以差殊觀也哉！吁！天人合其和節，事理通於幽明。知乎此，則可與同民心而出治道矣。
嘗攷，樂由天作，禮以地制，天地者禮樂之本也。聖王馭世，其始也法天地以為禮樂，其終也以禮樂而贊天地。要之，與道為一，故形之制作，無有乎弗合。後世拘拘器數，而不求端於天地，豈先王之意哉？故曰：「不聞性與天道，而能制禮作樂者，末矣。」
禮之先幣帛也，欲民之先事而後祿也。
陳思武
同考試官學正黃批：雅健精醇，記義之
translation_en:
…are not two wholly separate things. Viewed in their manifest aspect, they are called rites and music. The institution of rites adorns the governance of the realm; the creation of music proclaims its achievements. This is simply to make the unseen manifest in visible forms, revealing the sage’s consummate capacity. Viewed in their hidden aspect, they are called ghosts and spirits. When yin contracts, it concentrates its vital energy to bring about gathering and withdrawal; when yang expands, it releases its vital energy to bring about generation and growth. This is simply to conceal the visible within the unseen, rendering wondrous the workings of creation and transformation. In truth, rites and music, ghosts and spirits, are one principle. Thus music, which deepens harmony, follows the spirits and accords with Heaven; rites, which distinguish what is fitting, abide with the ghosts and accord with Earth. How could these be regarded as disparate? Ah! Heaven and humanity share their harmony and measured order; affairs and principles extend through both the hidden and the manifest. Those who understand this may be entrusted with unifying the people’s hearts and bringing forth the way of good government.
I have considered how music originates in Heaven and rites are patterned on Earth: Heaven and Earth are the foundations of rites and music. When sage kings govern the world, they begin by modeling rites and music on Heaven and Earth; in the end, through rites and music, they assist Heaven and Earth. In essence, they are one with the Way; thus, when they give it form in institutions, nothing fails to accord with it. Later generations fastidiously confine themselves to implements and numerical prescriptions without seeking their source in Heaven and Earth. Can this be what the former kings intended? Hence the saying: “There have never been [?] those who could institute rites and create music without having learned of human nature and the Way of Heaven.”
“Ritual observances precede gifts of silk because the intention is that the people should put service before emolument.”
Chen Siwu
Associate Examiner Huang, School Instructor, comments: “Elegant and vigorous, refined and pure; among interpretations of the meaning of the Book of Rites…”

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
最優者
考試官右中允孫批其詞達
考試官侍讀郭批充蔚可誦
君子盡乎交道者所以示民盡乎臣道也夫先
事後祿臣道之所當盡也君子盡交道以示之
其善牖民者乎坊記引夫子之言至此意謂世
教衰而民不興行義利之不明也久矣非君子
力爲之坊其流弊曷旣焉何則君子之相接必
有禮以致其敬亦必有幣帛以達其誠禮也幣
===
帛也貴於知所先後也後乎禮則徑情直行其
失也簡先乎幣帛則儀不及物其失也虛是故
恭敬以植其本而愿慤之意豫立於酬應之先
儀文以嘉其會而筐篚之陳斯行於辭讓之後
禮因物而將其將也爲中節物因禮而飾其飾
也爲合宜若此者豈直隆於交際而已哉意指
所在夫固廣義以教民焉耳夫禮者事之象幣
帛者祿之象君子先乎禮者蓋以先事之教示
天下使之效力宣猷惟汲汲於所當爲也後乎

所在夫固廣義以教民焉耳夫禮者事之象幣
帛者祿之象君子先乎禮者蓋以先事之教示
天下使之效力宣猷惟汲汲於所當爲也後乎

最優者。

考試官侍讀郭批：充蔚可誦。
君子盡乎交道者，所以示民盡乎臣道也。夫先事後祿，臣道之所當盡也。君子盡交道以示之，其善牖民者乎！《坊記》引夫子之言至此，意謂世教衰而民不興行，義利之不明也久矣。非君子力爲之坊，其流弊曷旣焉？何則？君子之相接，必有禮以致其敬，亦必有幣帛以達其誠。禮也，幣帛也，貴於知所先後也。後乎禮，則徑情直行，其失也簡；先乎幣帛，則儀不及物，其失也虛。是故恭敬以植其本，而愿慤之意豫立於酬應之先；儀文以嘉其會，而筐篚之陳斯行於辭讓之後。禮因物而將，其將也爲中節；物因禮而飾，其飾也爲合宜。若此者，豈直隆於交際而已哉？意指所在，夫固廣義以教民焉耳。夫禮者，事之象；幣帛者，祿之象。君子先乎禮者，蓋以先事之教示天下，使之效力宣猷，惟汲汲於所當爲也。後乎

…the finest.
Examiner Sun, Right Mentor, comments: “His language conveys his meaning clearly.”
Examiner Guo, Reader-in-Waiting, comments: “Rich and flourishing, worthy of recitation.”
The gentleman fulfills the proper way of social intercourse in order to show the people how to fulfill the proper way of serving as a minister. To put service before emolument is what a minister must fully accomplish. By fulfilling the proper way of social intercourse and thereby setting an example, is the gentleman not skilled at enlightening the people? In quoting the Master's words at this point, the chapter “Dikes” (Fangji) means that moral instruction in the world has declined and the people no longer bestir themselves to virtuous conduct: the distinction between righteousness and profit has long been unclear. Unless the gentleman strives to build a dike against this, how can its harmful consequences ever cease?
Why is this so? When gentlemen meet, they must observe ritual to express their respect, and they must also offer gifts of silk to convey their sincerity. With ritual and gifts of silk, what matters is knowing which should come first and which afterward. If ritual is put afterward, people act directly upon their feelings, and the fault is excessive simplicity; if gifts of silk are put first, ceremony falls short of the material offerings, and the fault is emptiness [?]. Thus reverence and respect establish the foundation, and an attitude of sincerity and integrity is formed before the exchange begins. Ceremonial forms lend grace to the meeting, and the presentation of baskets of gifts follows the courteous expressions of deference. Ritual is conveyed through material offerings, and its expression accords with the proper measure; material offerings are adorned through ritual, and their adornment accords with what is fitting. Is this merely a matter of making social intercourse more splendid? The underlying intention is surely to extend righteousness and thereby instruct the people.
Ritual symbolizes service; gifts of silk symbolize emolument. title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
幣帛者蓋以後祿之教示天下使之屏私防欲
不規規於所當得也敬爾有官亂爾有政黽勉
以奉其職而已矣若夫大言受大祿小言受小
祿固君之所以待臣焉者而豈可以預期乎進
思盡忠退思補過靖共以舉其分而已矣若夫
士而代耕大夫而食邑固上之所以厚下焉者
而豈可以預計乎是則先禮後物本出於賓主
酬應之常先事後祿因示乎義利重輕之辨上
執其機以教民如此民其庶幾從欲以治也哉
===
大抵君人馭衆肅之以令則難齊道之以德則
易格攷昔明王之世人多秉義而尚廉要之由
於上之所作禮先幣帛作於上矣民豈不蒸蒸
然應於下耶然必無所爲而爲斯可以言義使
或有意其間雖公亦私觀人者察其微焉爾已
第貳塲
論
聖人之心與天合一
方弘靜

第貳塲
論
聖人之心與天合一
方弘靜
translation_en:
…placing gifts of silk last teaches all under Heaven to put emoluments last, so that they set aside selfishness, guard against desire, and do not preoccupy themselves with what they ought to receive. “Attend reverently to your offices; administer your governmental duties”: they need only exert themselves diligently in fulfilling their offices. As for receiving great emoluments for great counsel and small emoluments for small counsel, this is indeed how a ruler treats his ministers; but how could they anticipate such rewards? When advancing into service, they think of giving their utmost loyalty; when withdrawing, they think of remedying their faults. They need only discharge their duties peacefully and reverently. As for officers receiving support in place of farming, and grand masters drawing revenues from fiefs, these are indeed ways in which superiors provide generously for their subordinates; but how could they calculate such benefits beforehand? Thus, placing ritual before material gifts originates in the ordinary exchanges between host and guest; placing service before emoluments thereby reveals the distinction between the greater weight of righteousness and the lesser weight of profit. If those above grasp this crucial means of teaching the people, might the people not then follow their desires and yet remain well governed?
Generally, when a ruler governs the multitude, it is difficult to bring them into order by imposing discipline through commands, but easy to bring them to what is right by guiding them through virtue. Examining the ages of the enlightened kings of old, we find that people commonly upheld righteousness and esteemed integrity. In essence, this arose from the example set by those above. When those above set the example of placing ritual before gifts of silk, how could the people below fail to respond with increasing enthusiasm? Yet only when one acts without an ulterior purpose can one speak of righteousness. If some calculated intention intervenes, even what is public-spirited becomes selfish. Those who judge people must simply scrutinize these subtle distinctions.
Second Session
Discourse
“The Mind of the Sage Is One with Heaven”
Fang Hongjing

The sages use ritual to restrain the world, and in instituting ritual they take Heaven as their basis. Is Heaven not the source of ritual? The distinctions between high and low, manifold and diverse, neither injuring nor conflicting with one another, have already been brilliantly displayed; yet people do not understand them. Thus the work of restraining the world must depend upon the sages. When a sage arises, he considers that Heaven has entrusted him with responsibility for restraining the world. Accordingly, he sets forth its norms, examines its measures and regulations, and guides the people of the world, confining them within the bounds of ritual and deference. Everyone says that ritual was instituted by the sages, without knowing that its origin lies in Heaven. title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
天之所獨厚是故制禮坊世之責必畀於聖人
聖人自知爲天民先覺有不得而辭其責者是
故皇皇焉制禮坊世以求合於天此禮之所由
起也書曰天叙有典勅我五典五惇哉天秩有
禮自我五禮有庸哉夫叙曰天叙秩曰天秩聖
人惇庸焉耳矣本非有所加於天也是故達之
乎朝廷之上布之乎海宇之廣釋回增美措正
施行君令而不違臣共而不貳父慈而教子孝
而箴兄愛而友弟敬而順夫和而義妻柔而正
===

道經緯萬端無所不貫者也爲之旂旟鸞纓以
繁其飾爲之火龍黼黻以著其章爲之朱絃疏
越以節其情爲之圭璧羔鴈以通其信進退有
度登降有儀文物以紀之聲名以發之是禮之
散殊所謂房皇周浹曲直得次第者也自天而
言則其統體如太和元氣運於冲漠其散殊如
五氣順布四時錯行百嘉鬯遂萬物蕃育也至
於時極勢窮人情不安其故不得已而通變損

translation_en:
…uniquely favored by Heaven. Thus the responsibility for instituting ritual and restraining the world must be entrusted to the sages. The sages know themselves to be the first among Heaven’s people to awaken to understanding, and cannot decline this responsibility. They therefore diligently institute ritual and restrain the world, seeking accord with Heaven. This is how ritual originated. The Book of Documents says: “Heaven has ordered the constant relationships; it charges us to make these five constant relationships steadfast! Heaven has ranked the rites; through us let these five rites have their regular observance!” Ordering is called Heaven’s ordering, and ranking is called Heaven’s ranking: the sages merely make these steadfast and put them into practice. They do not originally add anything to Heaven.

Thus ritual is extended to the imperial court and spread throughout the realm, dispelling perversity, enhancing goodness, establishing correctness, and putting it into practice. The ruler issues commands without departing from what is right; ministers are respectful and undivided in loyalty; fathers are loving and instructive; sons are filial and offer admonition; elder brothers are loving and friendly; younger brothers are respectful and obedient; husbands are harmonious and righteous; wives are gentle and upright. Among the multitudes of the people, none fails sincerely to accord with the supreme standard. This is ritual in its integral unity: what is meant by the warp and weft of the human way, running through its myriad affairs and leaving nothing unpervaded.

For them are made dragon and bird banners, carriage bells, and harness tassels, to enrich their adornment; fire, dragon, axe-head, and paired angular patterns, to display their insignia; red strings and widely spaced sound holes on zithers, to moderate their feelings; and jade tablets and disks, lambs and wild geese, to communicate their good faith. Advancing and retreating have their prescribed measures; ascending and descending have their proper forms. Ceremonial objects regulate these practices, and sounds and designations give them expression. This is ritual in its differentiated particulars: what is meant by its encompassing and penetrating all things, with the crooked and the straight each finding their proper order.

Speaking in terms of Heaven, ritual’s integral unity resembles the primordial vital energy of Supreme Harmony moving through the empty stillness; its differentiated particulars resemble the five vital energies spreading in due order, the four seasons proceeding in alternation, all flourishing things growing freely to fulfillment, and the myriad beings multiplying and developing. When the times reach their limit and circumstances are exhausted, and people’s feelings are no longer at ease with established practices, there is no choice but to adapt through change and make reductions…

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
蠢以作新之亦莫非禮猶之冬微暄夏微肅鼓
亭毒以妙化機而莫非天也蓋聖人心與天一
道與天侔是故履之而禮得制之而禮行先天
而天弗違後天而奉天時故太史公曰美哉洋
洋乎宰制萬物役使羣動豈人力也哉曰非人
力以見其合天也昔者齊桓晉文取威定霸挾
天子令諸侯然且下拜而不受請隧而不許以
共扶典禮於不墜韓宣子見周禮在魯則知周
所以王齊仲孫湫見魯秉周禮則知魯不可動
===
左氏釋經之例指某人某事曰禮也某人某事

人耳况春秋之世凌慢縱恣無所不至何至於
敬畏若此若此孔子稱君子畏天命畏聖人之
言夫畏天命固也至稱畏聖言無異天命則聖
人制禮坊世與天合一孔子蓋深識其心矣老
子詆禮爲忠信之薄荀卿詆聖人爲化性起僞
宋儒蘇洵乃云聖人制禮徒欲輕去其舊樂就

所以王齊仲孫湫見魯秉周禮則知魯不可動
===
左氏釋經之例指某人某事曰禮也某人某事
曰非禮也古之人惴惴焉惟恐犯禮豈非視禮
等於天乎如以禮爲聖人私智所出則聖人亦
人耳況春秋之世凌慢縱恣無所不至何至於
敬畏若此若此孔子稱君子畏天命畏聖人之
言夫畏天命固也至稱畏聖言無異天命則聖
人制禮坊世與天合一孔子蓋深識其心矣老
子詆禮爲忠信之薄荀卿詆聖人爲化性起僞
宋儒蘇洵乃云聖人制禮徒欲輕去其舊樂就
punctuated: 蠢，以作新之，亦莫非禮。猶之冬微暄、夏微肅，鼓亭毒以妙化機，而莫非天也。蓋聖人心與天一，道與天侔，是故履之而禮得，制之而禮行，先天而天弗違，後天而奉天時。故太史公曰：「美哉！洋洋乎！宰制萬物，役使羣動，豈人力也哉！」曰非人力，以見其合天也。昔者齊桓、晉文取威定霸，挾天子令諸侯，然且下拜而不受，請隧而不許，以共扶典禮於不墜。韓宣子見周禮在魯，則知周所以王；齊仲孫湫見魯秉周禮，則知魯不可動。左氏釋經之例，指某人某事曰「禮也」，某人某事曰「非禮也」。古之人惴惴焉，惟恐犯禮，豈非視禮等於天乎？如以禮爲聖人私智所出，則聖人亦人耳。况春秋之世，凌慢縱恣，無所不至，何至於敬畏若此若此？孔子稱：「君子畏天命，畏聖人之言。」夫畏天命固也，至稱畏聖言無異天命，則聖人制禮坊世，與天合一，孔子蓋深識其心矣。老子詆禮爲忠信之薄，荀卿詆聖人爲化性起僞，宋儒蘇洵乃云聖人制禮，徒欲輕去其舊，樂就
translation_en:
…[a doubtful character, 蠢, concludes the preceding phrase about modification and adjustment [?]] to renew it: this, too, is entirely ritual propriety. It is like a slight warmth in winter or a slight chill in summer, setting nurturing powers in motion to give subtle efficacy to the workings of transformation: all of this, too, is Heaven. The sage’s mind is one with Heaven, and his Way matches Heaven’s. Thus, through his practice, ritual propriety is rightly realized; through his institutions, it is put into effect. When he precedes Heaven, Heaven does not oppose him; when he follows Heaven, he observes Heaven’s seasons. Thus the Grand Astrologer said: “How beautiful! How vast! It governs the myriad things and directs all moving beings. Could this be the work of human effort?” In saying that it is not human effort, he reveals its accord with Heaven.

Formerly, Duke Huan of Qi and Duke Wen of Jin established their authority and secured hegemony, invoking the Son of Heaven to command the regional lords. Yet even then, a bow made below the hall was declined, and a request for a tomb passage was denied, thereby jointly upholding the ritual institutions against collapse. When Han Xuanzi saw that the rituals of Zhou survived in Lu, he understood how Zhou had attained kingship. When Zhongsun Jiao of Qi saw that Lu maintained the rituals of Zhou, he understood that Lu could not be shaken. Zuo’s practice in elucidating the Classic was to identify a particular person or deed and say, “This accords with ritual propriety,” or another person or deed and say, “This violates ritual propriety.” The people of antiquity were apprehensive, fearing only that they might transgress ritual propriety. Was this not because they regarded it as equal to Heaven?

If ritual propriety were understood as issuing from the sages’ private ingenuity, then the sages, too, were merely human. Moreover, in the Spring and Autumn period, arrogance and unbridled self-indulgence knew no bounds. Why, then, would reverence and fear have reached such a degree—such a degree? Confucius said: “The gentleman stands in awe of Heaven’s mandate and of the words of the sages.” That one should stand in awe of Heaven’s mandate is unquestionable. But to speak of awe for the sages’ words as no different from awe for Heaven’s mandate means that the sages, in instituting ritual to restrain the world, were united with Heaven. Confucius surely understood their intentions profoundly.

Laozi disparaged ritual as the thinning of loyalty and trustworthiness; Xun Qing disparaged the sages as transforming human nature and giving rise to deliberate artifice. The Song scholar Su Xun even said that the sages instituted ritual merely to make people readily abandon their old ways and gladly adopt…

text:
其法無故而使之事君事父謂有術焉以厭服
其心噫豈知禮者哉豈知聖人之心者哉故繩
墨誠陳不可欺以曲直權衡誠縣不可欺以輕
重規矩誠設不可欺以方圓聖人審於禮不可
欺以詐僞故不法禮不足禮者謂之無方之民
法禮足禮者謂之有方之民乃若以禮爲聖人
所獨擅古今所難與牽於繁文拘於小說一有
毫毛之差卽終身格而不行則又自絕於聖人
自棄其天者也嗚呼禮國之榦而民之紀也榦

punctuated:
其法，無故而使之事君事父，謂有術焉以厭服其心。噫！豈知禮者哉？豈知聖人之心者哉？故繩墨誠陳，不可欺以曲直；權衡誠縣，不可欺以輕重；規矩誠設，不可欺以方圓。聖人審於禮，不可欺以詐僞。故不法禮、不足禮者，謂之無方之民；法禮、足禮者，謂之有方之民。乃若以禮爲聖人所獨擅、古今所難與，牽於繁文，拘於小說，一有毫毛之差，卽終身格而不行，則又自絕於聖人、自棄其天者也。嗚呼！禮，國之榦而民之紀也。榦立則昌，紀正則治。載在簡冊，歷歷可稽。君人者必秉先王之禮，因時達宜，劑量損益，教化浹洽，民用和睦。以爲下則順，以爲上則安。天地以奠，日月以明，江河以流，萬物以育。禮豈不至矣哉？是之謂善希聖，是之謂善法天。

表

擬崇祀先聖先師於永明後殿，羣臣賀表。
translation_en:
…his rules, and, without cause, make them serve their rulers and fathers, asserting that there is a technique for subduing their hearts. Alas! Could such a person understand ritual? Could he understand the sages’ intentions? Thus, once the inked carpenter’s line is properly laid out, one cannot deceive it about crookedness and straightness; once the balance is properly suspended, one cannot deceive it about lightness and heaviness; once the compass and square are properly set out, one cannot deceive them about squareness and roundness. The sage is discerning in ritual and cannot be deceived by fraud or artifice. Thus, those who neither take ritual as their rule nor fulfill its requirements are called people without standards; those who take ritual as their rule and fulfill its requirements are called people with standards. Yet those who regard ritual as the exclusive province of sages, beyond the reach of people past and present, who become entangled in elaborate formalities and constrained by petty interpretations, and who, at the slightest discrepancy, remain obstructed for life and fail to act—these, too, cut themselves off from the sages and abandon their own Heaven-given nature. Alas! Ritual is the supporting trunk of the state and the guiding order of the people. When the trunk stands firm, the state flourishes; when the guiding order is correct, good government prevails. This is recorded in books and can be verified in clear detail. Those who rule others must uphold the ritual of the former kings, respond to the times and discern what is fitting, and weigh what should be reduced or added. Moral instruction will then permeate society, and the people will live in harmony. Through ritual, those below are obedient and those above are secure. Through it, Heaven and Earth are settled, the sun and moon shine, rivers flow, and all things are nurtured. Is ritual not the highest perfection? This is what is meant by aspiring well to sagehood; this is what is meant by modeling oneself well on Heaven.

Memorial

Draft congratulatory memorial from the assembled officials on honoring the Former Sage and Former Teacher with sacrifices in the rear hall of Yongming.

伏以，黃道天開，海宇被文明之化；紫宸地切，聖師增俎豆之光。舉曠典於千年，修上儀於一代。聲馳遐邇，喜溢臣工。臣等誠懽誠抃，稽首頓首。竊惟大道無爲，必因人而寄統；聖人有作，務傳道以覺民。懿軌弗磨，芳圖歷紀。羲農制器，寔成天地之能；黃帝垂衣，蓋取乾坤之象。唐堯一中授受，式開道學之原；虞舜四語丁寧，益闡淵微之旨。勤儉允賢乎大禹，寬仁用賛於成湯。
translation_en:
Zhang Hanxiang

Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor: “Elegant parallel prose, refined and orderly, dazzling to the eye. A fine scholar! A fine scholar!”

Comment by Associate Examiner Pan, Instructor: “He integrates the classics and arranges his material methodically, thoroughly grasping the form of the memorial.”

Comment by Examiner Sun, Right Companion to the Heir Apparent: “Savoring the blossoms and chewing their finest essence: an excellent memorial.”

Comment by Examiner Guo, Reader-in-Waiting: “Classical and elegant.”

We humbly submit: Heaven opens the imperial path, and all within the seas receives the transforming influence of cultivated enlightenment; the Purple Palace lies close at hand, and the sage teachers gain added splendor through sacrificial offerings. You have enacted a ceremony unparalleled in a thousand years and performed the highest rites of this age. Its renown spreads far and near; joy overflows among your officials. We, your servants, truly rejoice and clap our hands, bowing our heads and knocking our foreheads upon the ground.

We humbly reflect that the Great Way acts without action, yet must entrust its succession to human beings; when sages arise, they strive to transmit the Way and enlighten the people. Their exemplary patterns remain undiminished; their glorious designs endure through the ages. Fuxi and Shennong fashioned implements, truly bringing to fulfillment the capacities of Heaven and Earth. Huangdi let his robes hang down in effortless rule, taking his models from Qian and Kun, Heaven and Earth. Yao of Tang handed down the single principle of the Mean, thereby opening the source of learning the Way; Shun of Yu earnestly enjoined his four sayings, further elucidating its profound and subtle meaning. Great Yu was truly worthy in diligence and frugality; Cheng Tang was praised for generosity and benevolence…

丕顯文謨，易彖之陳具在；丕承武烈，丹書之戒猶存。典禮修明，姬旦思兼三聖；斯文未喪，宣尼道載六經。垂世教而淑人心，植天經而扶地紀。是皆可模可範，足稱先聖先師，宜隆崇報之儀，乃遡源流之正。慨自淳龐既散，意指漸乖，尚功利者殊隔藩籬，騁詞華者未窺閫奧。心法不沿於大統，治理僅見其小康。墜緒無傳，昌期有待。
恭惟皇帝陛下，乾剛天賦，離照日升。建皇極以叙彞倫，觀會通而行典禮。淵衷敬一，演註五箴；睿性聰明，旁搜羣籍。掀揭丕昭乎功業，經緯煥發於文章。萬方仰敷錫之休，八表囿雍熙之俗。是蓋誕膺
translation_en:
…Greatly manifest were King Wen’s designs, whose exposition remains fully preserved in the judgments of the Book of Changes; greatly continued were King Wu’s achievements, and the admonitions of the Cinnabar Writing still survive. Ritual institutions were cultivated and clarified: Ji Dan’s thought encompassed that of the three sages. This cultural tradition was not lost: the Way of Xuanni—Confucius—was recorded in the Six Classics. They handed down teachings for the world and made people’s hearts good, establishing Heaven’s enduring norms and sustaining Earth’s ordering principles. All these figures may serve as models and exemplars, deserving to be called former sages and former teachers. It is fitting to exalt the rites that honor and requite them, thereby tracing the tradition to its true source. Alas, once pristine simplicity had dispersed, its meaning and purport gradually diverged. Those who prized achievement and profit remained far outside its enclosing walls; those who displayed literary brilliance never glimpsed its inner chambers. The methods of cultivating the mind were no longer transmitted through the great succession, and government achieved only a modest degree of order. The broken thread of the tradition found no transmitter; an age of flourishing remained to be awaited.
We reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor is endowed by Heaven with the strength of Qian, and that your illumination, like Li, rises with the sun. You establish the august standard to order the constant human relationships, and discern how things converge and connect in carrying out canonical rites. In your profound heart you revere unity, expounding and annotating the Five Admonitions; endowed with sagely intelligence, you search widely through the collected writings. Your achievements stand forth in great splendor, and your ordering principles shine brilliantly in your writings. The myriad regions look up to the blessings you bestow, and all eight horizons embrace customs of harmony and prosperity. This is surely because you have grandly received…

峻命，眞傳遠契帝王，祗踐先猷，正學同符周孔。心神曠世而相感，情文因舊以加詳。
龍闕東南，地爲中禁，鳳池密邇。殿曰永明，睹縟典於告成，閱精禋於有楚。虹霓散彩，上干霄漢之清虚；金碧交輝，下燭戶庭之偉麗。一脉永聯於今古，四座不紊乎君臣。近接史宬，石室圖書之府；前瞻宗廟，金輿陟降之區。歲時嚴釋奠之將，朔望重輔臣之遣。羹牆有見，嚮慕彌勤。此我皇上制作超百王，而風聲示四海者也。
臣等清班久列，寵澤均霑。幸吾道之泰來，慶斯文之鼎重。奎光定現，聯東壁之星躔；勝事當書，秉左圽之史筆。心寔顓於頌述，詞莫罄於揄揚。伏願世教休明，人文宣朗，道已至而益至，
translation_en:
…the lofty mandate. The true transmission accords across the ages with the ancient emperors and kings; reverently following the plans of his predecessors, his orthodox learning tallies with that of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius. Their minds and spirits respond to one another across generations; sentiments and ceremonial forms follow ancient precedent while receiving further elaboration.
Southeast of the imperial palace, within the inner precincts and close beside the Phoenix Pool, stands a hall called Yongming. At its completion, elaborate ceremonies were witnessed, and pure sacrificial offerings were displayed in orderly array. Rainbow colors spread upward into the clear expanses of the heavens; gold and jade-green hues shine together, illuminating the magnificence of its gates and courts below. A single line of transmission forever joins past and present; the four seats preserve the distinctions between sovereign and subject. Nearby stands the imperial archive, a stone chamber housing books and documents; before it lies the ancestral temple, the precinct where the golden imperial carriage comes and goes. At the appointed seasons, the presentation of offerings to the sages is solemnly conducted; at each new and full moon, particular importance is attached to dispatching assisting ministers. As though seeing the sages in his soup and upon the wall, his longing and admiration grow ever more earnest. Such are the institutions established by our Emperor, surpassing those of the hundred kings, and the exemplary influence he displays throughout the Four Seas.
We, your servants, have long held places in the ranks of distinguished officials and have shared alike in your gracious favor. We rejoice that our Way has entered an age of flourishing and celebrate the great esteem accorded to this cultural tradition. The radiance of the Kui constellation assuredly appears, joining the celestial course of the Eastern Wall constellation. This splendid event deserves to be recorded, wielding the historian’s brush of Zuo [?]. Our hearts are wholly devoted to praise and commemoration, yet words cannot exhaust our acclaim. We humbly wish that the teachings guiding the world may flourish in brilliance, that human culture may shine forth, and that the Way, already brought to perfection, may attain still greater perfection…

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
皇祖創業之隆
皇上中興之盛其涵濡治化獨深者與
考試官侍讀郭批統朔自三代後未有如我
國家之正而
功德尤盛焉此策據古陳詞敷揚精確必有學有識之士也
自天下有正統而後人君之位尊自天下
有正朔而後朝廷之政一蓋正也者所以
正天下之不正也繫統於正則定是非示
褒貶以伸一王之法而假名僭號者舉不
===
得以紊真矣繫朔於正則明好尚新耳目

考試官侍讀郭批：統朔自三代後，未有如我國家之正，而功德尤盛焉。此策據古陳詞，敷揚精確，必有學有識之士也。

自天下有正統，而後人君之位尊；自天下有正朔，而後朝廷之政一。蓋正也者，所以正天下之不正也。繫統於正，則定是非、示褒貶，以伸一王之法，而假名僭號者舉不得以紊真矣；繫朔於正，則明好尚、新耳目，以定一代之制，而竊據偏安者舉不得以干紀矣。然正統一也，有能用夏變夷、闢邪崇正，建不拔之殊勛，則扶植彞倫，為萬代所瞻仰；正朔一也，有能應時之正、順令之善，立不易之常道，則劑量今古，為百世所遵行。此我太祖高皇帝暨我皇上神功聖德，視古帝王有光，而漢唐宋皆莫
translation_en:
…the grandeur of our imperial ancestor’s founding achievement and the splendor of His Majesty’s restoration. Has the author not been exceptionally deeply imbued with the transforming influence of this government?

Examiner Guo, Reader-in-waiting, comments: Since the Three Dynasties, no dynastic succession or calendar has possessed legitimacy equal to that of our dynasty, whose achievements and virtue are especially magnificent. This policy essay draws upon antiquity to make its case and expounds its praises with precision. Its author must be a man of learning and discernment.

Only once legitimate dynastic succession exists under Heaven is the ruler’s position exalted; only once an authoritative calendar exists under Heaven is the court’s government unified. For legitimacy serves to rectify whatever is not rightful under Heaven. To ground succession in legitimacy is to determine right and wrong and make praise and blame manifest, thereby upholding the laws of a sovereign, so that none who assume false designations or usurp titles can confound the true succession. To ground the calendar in legitimacy is to clarify what is esteemed and renew what people hear and see, thereby establishing the institutions of a dynasty, so that none who seize territory and content themselves with holding a corner of the realm can violate its governing order.

Yet although legitimate succession is one and the same in principle, a ruler who can transform the barbarians through Chinese civilization, reject the deviant and honor the correct, and establish extraordinary achievements that cannot be undone thereby sustains the enduring moral relationships and wins the admiration of countless generations. Although the authoritative calendar is one and the same in principle, a ruler who can respond correctly to the seasons, follow the excellence of their ordinances, and establish an unchanging, enduring Way thereby weighs past and present and provides a standard for a hundred generations to follow. Thus the divine achievements and sagely virtue of our Emperor Taizu Gao and our present emperor shine beside those of the ancient emperors and kings, while the Han, Tang, and Song all fail to…

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之及也與請敬陳之三代以上禪授征伐
或以至公或以大義皆得天下之正然未
嘗有正統之名唐虞之世觀文察變日中
星鳥以殷仲春寔得人時之正然未嘗有
正朔之名厥後王室衰微乾綱解紐諸侯
強背治道日湮是故由不正與不一而正
統正朔之名始立於天下矣正統之說本
乎春秋春秋曰春王正月又凡下聘出狩
皆冠之曰天王夫於正必書王於王必稱
===
天僭竊之邦則降而書人書子即世所未
明者闕之不亦微矣乎由周以降君天下
而得附於正統者有漢唐宋焉漢取其誅
無道秦唐取其平隋亂宋取其混一五季
致治有功保治無失君子所以皆與之統
歐陽脩著正統論其大致謂堯舜以來統
三絕而三續自周亡迄于顯德可疑之際
有三以合天下於一者皆與之統而獨黜
三國南北朝及五代蘇軾祖其說發為貴

punctuated:
之及也與？請敬陳之。三代以上，禪授征伐，或以至公，或以大義，皆得天下之正，然未嘗有正統之名。唐虞之世，觀文察變，日中星鳥，以殷仲春，寔得人時之正，然未嘗有正朔之名。厥後王室衰微，乾綱解紐，諸侯強背，治道日湮。是故由不正與不一，而正統正朔之名始立於天下矣。

正統之說本乎《春秋》。《春秋》曰：「春王正月。」又凡下聘出狩，皆冠之曰「天王」。夫於正必書王，於王必稱天；僭竊之邦，則降而書人、書子；即世所未明者，闕之，不亦微矣乎？由周以降，君天下而得附於正統者，有漢、唐、宋焉。漢取其誅無道秦，唐取其平隋亂，宋取其混一五季。致治有功，保治無失，君子所以皆與之統。歐陽脩著《正統論》，其大致謂堯舜以來，統三絕而三續；自周亡迄于顯德，可疑之際有三。以合天下於一者皆與之統，而獨黜三國、南北朝及五代。蘇軾祖其說，發為貴
translation_en:
…could any of the Han, Tang, or Song equal them? Allow me respectfully to set forth the matter. In the Three Dynasties and earlier, transfers of the throne and punitive conquests proceeded either from supreme impartiality or from great righteousness. All thus rightly acquired rule over All under Heaven, yet the term “legitimate succession” had not yet arisen. In the age of Tang Yao and Yu Shun, they observed celestial patterns and examined their changes: “The day is of middle length, and the star is the Bird,” by which they determined mid-spring. They truly established the proper seasons for human activity, yet the term “official calendar” had not yet arisen. Thereafter, the royal house declined, the bonds of sovereign authority unraveled, the feudal lords grew powerful and rebellious, and the way of good government became increasingly obscured. Thus it was because legitimacy and unity were lacking that the terms “legitimate succession” and “official calendar” first came to be established in the world.

The doctrine of legitimate succession originates in the Spring and Autumn Annals. The Annals says: “Spring, the king’s first month.” Moreover, whenever it records the dispatch of envoys on courtesy missions to the feudal lords or the king’s departure on a tour of inspection, it invariably prefixes the designation “Heavenly King.” In mentioning the first month, it necessarily writes “king”; in mentioning the king, it necessarily invokes Heaven. As for states that usurped authority, it demotes their rulers by writing “man” or “viscount”; where matters were unclear to the world, it leaves them unrecorded [?]. Is this not subtle indeed? From the Zhou onward, those who ruled All under Heaven and qualified for inclusion in the legitimate succession were the Han, Tang, and Song. The Han is accepted because it punished the tyrannical Qin; the Tang because it quelled the disorders of the Sui; and the Song because it unified the realm after the Five Dynasties. They achieved good government and preserved it without failing: this is why the gentleman grants all of them a place in the succession. Ouyang Xiu wrote the Discourse on Legitimate Succession. Its general argument is that, since Yao and Shun, the succession had been broken three times and restored three times; from the fall of the Zhou down to the Xiande reign period, there were three periods of uncertainty. He granted a place in the succession to all who united All under Heaven, excluding only the Three Kingdoms, the Northern and Southern Dynasties, and the Five Dynasties. Su Shi took this doctrine as his foundation and elaborated it through an analogy concerning the noble…

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
賤賢不肖之喻帝王人氏之辨所以闢章
子之說之非以輔歐陽氏正統之論惟朱
熹作綱目進昭烈黜曹魏為得尊王之義
然周秦晉漢隋唐皆以正統與之後世有
遺論焉傳曰天下有正統亦有變統所謂
變統者取之不以仁義如晉宋齊梁之君
即使混一區宇亦不得為正守之不以仁
義如秦如隋即使傳世數百亦不得為正
夫變統之名立則正統之說明而予奪勸
===
戒之道釐然可見矣是故歷代之統當以
五帝三王為正而漢唐宋次之假名僭號
者舉不足以紊真至若胡元之亂華腥羶
我宇宙犬羊我人民謂之無統可也况得
上附於先王之正統也哉正朔之善質諸
孔子孔子曰行夏之時又曰吾得夏時焉
蓋以夏正建寅盛德在木為生物之始為
改歲之端即人所共見者用之不亦善矣
乎由夏以降君天下而迭建乎正朔者有

子之說之非以輔歐陽氏正統之論惟朱
熹作綱目進昭烈黜曹魏爲得尊王之義

===

五帝三王爲正而漢唐宋次之假名僭號
者舉不足以紊眞至若胡元之亂華羶禮
我宇宙犬羊我人民謂之無統可也况得

改歲之端即人所共見者用之不亦善矣
乎由夏以降君天下而迭建乎正朔者有
punctuated:
賤賢不肖之喻、帝王人氏之辨，所以闢章子之說之非，以輔歐陽氏正統之論。惟朱熹作《綱目》，進昭烈，黜曹魏，為得尊王之義。然周秦晉漢隋唐皆以正統與之，後世有遺論焉。傳曰：「天下有正統，亦有變統。」所謂變統者，取之不以仁義，如晉宋齊梁之君，即使混一區宇，亦不得為正；守之不以仁義，如秦如隋，即使傳世數百，亦不得為正。夫變統之名立，則正統之說明，而予奪勸戒之道釐然可見矣。是故歷代之統，當以五帝三王為正，而漢唐宋次之。假名僭號者，舉不足以紊真。至若胡元之亂華，腥羶我宇宙，犬羊我人民，謂之無統可也，况得上附於先王之正統也哉！
正朔之善，質諸孔子。孔子曰：「行夏之時。」又曰：「吾得夏時焉。」蓋以夏正建寅，盛德在木，為生物之始，為改歲之端，即人所共見者用之，不亦善矣乎？由夏以降，君天下而迭建乎正朔者有
translation_en:
…the analogy of noble and base, worthy and unworthy, and the distinction between emperors and kings and ordinary persons [?], thereby refuting the errors of Master Zhang’s account and supporting Ouyang Xiu’s argument concerning legitimate succession. Zhu Xi alone, in composing the Outline and Details (Gangmu), elevated Emperor Zhaolie and excluded Cao Wei, thus capturing the principle of honoring the rightful king. Yet he accorded legitimate succession to Zhou, Qin, Jin, Han, Sui, and Tang alike, leaving matters for later generations to debate. A transmitted account says: “Under Heaven there is legitimate succession, and there is also irregular succession.” What is meant by irregular succession is this: those who acquire the realm without benevolence and righteousness, such as the rulers of Jin, Song, Qi, and Liang, cannot be considered legitimate even if they unite the entire realm; those who maintain possession of it without benevolence and righteousness, such as Qin and Sui, cannot be considered legitimate even if their dynasties endure for several hundred years. Once the category of irregular succession is established, the doctrine of legitimate succession becomes clear, and the principles of granting and withholding recognition, encouraging and admonishing, become plainly apparent. Thus, in judging succession through the ages, the Five Emperors and Three Kings should be deemed fully legitimate, with Han, Tang, and Song ranking next. Those who falsely assumed names and usurped titles are altogether incapable of confounding genuine legitimacy. As for the barbarian Yuan, which threw Chinese civilization into disorder, befouled our world with the stench of raw meat and mutton, and treated our people like dogs and sheep, it may properly be said to have had no legitimate succession at all. How much less could it be ranked with the legitimate succession of the former kings!
The merits of the calendar and the beginning of the year may be assessed by reference to Confucius. Confucius said: “Follow the seasons of Xia.” He also said: “I obtained the calendar of Xia.” This is because the first month of the Xia calendar corresponds to the earthly branch yin, when the flourishing potency lies in Wood: it is the beginning of the generation of living things and the starting point of the new year. Is it not good to adopt what everyone can observe? From Xia onward, among those who ruled all under Heaven and successively established their calendars were…

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
商周焉商以丑月爲歲首周以子月爲歲
首天開於子地闢於丑聖王所以皆建之
朔葉時著正朔解其大致謂三代歲首不
同而夏時紀月則一引商書元祀三祀之
文周禮太史馮相氏之職反覆辯論周以
子月爲正則四時錯亂曆數何由而定日
月星辰何由而驗蔡沈祖其說亦曰周人

translation_en:
…there were the Shang and Zhou. The Shang took the month designated chou as the beginning of the year, while the Zhou took the month designated zi. Heaven opened at zi, and earth unfolded at chou; this is why the sage kings established these as the beginnings of their years. Ye Shi wrote the Explanation of the Calendar’s First Month. His general argument was that although the Three Dynasties began their years differently, they were alike in reckoning the months according to the Xia seasons. Citing the passages concerning the first and third years of sacrifice in the Documents of Shang, and the duties of the Grand Scribe and the Astrologer in the Rites of Zhou, he argued at length: if the Zhou made the zi month their first month, the four seasons would fall into disorder. How, then, could calendrical calculations be established? How could the movements of the sun, moon, and stars be verified? Cai Shen followed this explanation, likewise saying that the Zhou established zi as the beginning and merely took the tenth month [?] as the start of the year, while their seasons and months all retained the old Xia reckoning. Hu Anguo alone, in his commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals, concluded that Xia seasonal designations were placed before Zhou month numbers, a judgment regarded as striking a balance among the various explanations.

Yet Confucius was a man of Zhou and once said, “I follow Zhou.” If, without occupying the requisite position, he had altered the Zhou calendar, how could he have instructed all under Heaven? Scholars have been deeply perplexed by this. The Commentary says: “In the twentieth year of Duke Zhao, in spring, in the first month, on the jichou day, the sun reached its southernmost point”; and “In the fifth year of Duke Xi, in the first month, on the xinhai day, the sun reached its southernmost point.” Now the sun reaches its southernmost point in winter, in the eleventh month of the Xia calendar, yet these passages say “spring” and “first month.” Thus it is perfectly clear that the Zhou calendar changed both the seasonal designations and the month numbers.

Therefore, among the calendars of successive dynasties, the Xia calendar, which established yin as the first month, should be regarded as the proper standard, with those of Shang and Zhou ranked next. Those who usurped territory or maintained rule over only a portion of the realm are altogether unworthy of interfering with the calendrical order. As for the Qin of the Ying lineage, which established hai as the first month, by then the vital energies had already become closed off and winter had arrived; nevertheless, they began the year at that point and…

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
名春謂之無朔可也豈得上附於前代之
正朔也哉我
太祖高皇帝救民伐罪用夏變夷建開闢所未
有之功還帝王所自立之地三綱既墜而
復振九法既斁而復修所謂取以仁義守
以仁義者也永清禹甸以繫四海之人心
酌用夏時以示一代之觀聽是其得統之
正上繼先王頒朔之善下垂後世功德隆
盛邈乎無以尚之矣

名春，謂之無朔可也，豈得上附於前代之正朔也哉？我太祖高皇帝救民伐罪，用夏變夷，建開闢所未有之功，還帝王所自立之地。三綱既墜而復振，九法既斁而復修，所謂取以仁義、守以仁義者也。永清禹甸，以繫四海之人心；酌用夏時，以示一代之觀聽。是其得統之正，上繼先王；頒朔之善，下垂後世。功德隆盛，邈乎無以尚之矣。

列聖相承，引而弗替，治平之業基於無窮。肆我皇上以元聖之資，撫中興之運，圖維治理，二十五年于茲。一德以格天，三重以立極，祀郊以明禮，尊親以盡倫，憫農以恤災，飭兵以備患，洽化以同俗，弘業以垂休。凡所以陋前代而遵
translation_en:
…and called it spring. One may call this having no legitimate calendar at all; how could it rank alongside the calendrical systems of preceding dynasties? Our Emperor Taizu Gao rescued the people and punished the guilty, transforming the barbarians through the ways of the Xia. He accomplished deeds unprecedented since the beginning of the world and restored the lands where the sage emperors and kings had established their rule. He revived the Three Bonds after their collapse and restored the Nine Principles of government after their corruption. This is what is meant by acquiring rule through benevolence and righteousness and preserving it through benevolence and righteousness. He forever pacified the domains of Yu, securing the allegiance of people throughout the realm; he judiciously adopted the Xia calendar, setting an example for the eyes and ears of an entire age. Thus the legitimacy of his succession continued the legacy of the former kings, while the excellence of his promulgation of the calendar furnished a model for later generations. His achievements and virtue were so magnificent that nothing could surpass them.

The successive sage emperors carried this forward without letting it lapse, laying foundations for orderly and peaceful government that would endure forever. Thus our present emperor, endowed with the qualities of a supreme sage and presiding over an era of dynastic resurgence, has devoted himself to good government for twenty-five years now. Through undivided virtue he reaches Heaven; through the three weighty responsibilities of rulership he establishes the supreme standard. He performs the suburban sacrifices to make ritual propriety manifest and honors his parents to fulfill the duties of human relationships. He has compassion for farmers and brings relief in disasters; he puts the armed forces in order to prepare against dangers. translation_en:
…the imperial ancestor: these manifold measures of good government cannot be exhaustively recounted. As for abolishing sacrifices to the barbarian Yuan rulers to uphold human moral order, this was a great achievement in sustaining the legitimate succession; and performing the di sacrifice to the Lord on High to establish Heaven’s enduring order preserved the principle of honoring the legitimate calendar. These are indeed things seldom heard of since antiquity, which the imperial ancestor had not fully accomplished and which awaited the present day. May the continuation of the imperial succession endure without limit, like Heaven; may the realm that observes the imperial calendar extend without bounds, like the earth. How fortunate I am to witness this flourishing age in person! Respectfully submitted in reply.

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
略夫建非常之勛者必達通變之宜締不
拔之業者必思經久之術慕高遠之略而
忽酌時之務不可以言變襲故常之迹而
無敦本之實不可以言久故酌時者達幾
者也敦本者審勢者也此忠臣謀佐所宜
日夜孜孜集衆思而廣忠益以殷邦永治
者也於乎三代之迹邈矣後世近古者其
兩漢之治乎上下之經畫史冊之紀載文
治武功之外無異說也是故良吏爲盛而
===
名將輩出唐宋鮮儷焉
國家創法定制濊澤深仁匹三代而軼兩漢
百有七十餘年生齒蕃茂邊圉寧謐稱治
安矣邇來田野賦稅荒逋日甚徵役煩多
財力告匱夷虜驕而頻肆蹂掠士馬罷而
扞禦靡績內之安養外之經畫視昔富彊
不無少遜焉執事亦思而得其故乎內地
之政名實相眩更張太易而人鮮定守有
教養之名而無教養之實無惑乎民生之

略。夫建非常之勛者，必達通變之宜；締不拔之業者，必思經久之術。慕高遠之略而忽酌時之務，不可以言變；襲故常之迹而無敦本之實，不可以言久。故酌時者，達幾者也；敦本者，審勢者也。此忠臣謀佐所宜日夜孜孜，集衆思而廣忠益，以殷邦永治者也。於乎！三代之迹邈矣，後世近古者，其兩漢之治乎？上下之經畫，史冊之紀載，文治武功之外無異說也。是故良吏爲盛，而名將輩出，唐宋鮮儷焉。
國家創法定制，濊澤深仁，匹三代而軼兩漢。百有七十餘年，生齒蕃茂，邊圉寧謐，稱治安矣。邇來田野賦稅荒逋日甚，徵役煩多，財力告匱；夷虜驕而頻肆蹂掠，士馬罷而扞禦靡績。內之安養，外之經畫，視昔富彊，不無少遜焉。執事亦思而得其故乎？內地之政，名實相眩，更張太易，而人鮮定守；有教養之名，而無教養之實，無惑乎民生之
translation_en:
…an outline. Those who establish extraordinary achievements must understand how best to adapt to changing circumstances; those who lay foundations that cannot be shaken must consider methods that will endure. To admire lofty and far-reaching strategies while neglecting the practical task of weighing present circumstances is no basis for speaking of adaptation. To follow established precedents without actually strengthening the foundations is no basis for speaking of endurance. Thus, those who weigh present circumstances understand the first signs of change; those who strengthen the foundations assess the configuration of affairs. These are matters on which loyal ministers and counselors should labor diligently day and night, gathering the thoughts of many and extending the benefits of loyal counsel, so that the realm may prosper and remain well governed forever. Alas! The accomplishments of the Three Dynasties are remote indeed. Among later ages, was it not the government of the two Han dynasties that came closest to antiquity? In the plans of rulers and ministers, and in the accounts preserved in the histories, there is nothing to discuss beyond civil governance and military achievement. Hence able officials flourished and renowned generals appeared in succession; the Tang and Song seldom matched them.
Our dynasty established laws and institutions, bestowing abundant blessings and profound benevolence, matching the Three Dynasties and surpassing the two Han dynasties. For more than a hundred and seventy years, the population has multiplied and the frontiers have been tranquil: this may be called orderly and peaceful government. Recently, however, neglect and arrears in rural tax payments have worsened daily, levies and labor services have become burdensome and numerous, and financial resources have been exhausted. The foreign foes grow arrogant and repeatedly ravage and plunder, while our troops and horses are weary and achieve little in defense. In providing peace and sustenance within and planning for affairs beyond the frontiers, we fall somewhat short of our former wealth and strength. Have you, honored examiners, reflected on this and discovered its cause? In the administration of the interior, nominal claims and actual performance are confused; changes are made too readily, and few maintain a settled course. There is the name of educating and sustaining the people, but none of its substance. It is no wonder that the people's livelihood…

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
未遂也邊方之政文法是縻玩愒成習而
警備頗疎有戰守之具而無戰守之實無
惑乎武功之弗振也夫內外相須乆矣內
不安則無以奮攘外之威外不攘則無以
底安內之績謀國者重內而忽外固不可
急外而略內尤不可也愚嘗論今日之勢
矣內如扶弱補羸所宜安頤休息而奔突
勞頓則悖也外如拯溺救焚所宜攘袂奮
臂而紓徐退遜則後也中外奉法之臣救
偏葺敝幾倖目前而乏眞確乆遠之圖守
故襲常攘譽嫁咎而無協恭弘濟之實豈
不繆哉議者曰安內在擇吏是也今郡縣
之官豈無廉平豈弟如龔遂之在勃海黃
霸之在潁川召信臣之在南陽文翁之在
蜀郡者乎有之未必盡陟而貪鄙苟且飾
虛譽恡實惠者或得以冒遷而規黜此吏
治之所以弗勸也是故復乆任以固其志
精考課以稽其政嚴舉刺以甄其類公黜

不繆哉議者曰安內在擇吏是也今郡縣
之官豈無廉平豈弟如龔遂之在勃海黃
霸之在潁川召信臣之在南陽文翁之在
蜀郡者乎有之未必盡然而貪鄙苟且飾
虛譽格實惠者或得以冒遷而覬黜此吏
治之所以弗勸也是故復久任以固其志
精考課以稽其政嚴舉刺以甄其類公黜
punctuated:
未遂也。邊方之政，文法是縻，玩愒成習，而警備頗疎；有戰守之具，而無戰守之實，無惑乎武功之弗振也。夫內外相須乆矣，內不安則無以奮攘外之威，外不攘則無以底安內之績。謀國者，重內而忽外固不可，急外而略內尤不可也。愚嘗論今日之勢矣：內如扶弱補羸，所宜安頤休息，而奔突勞頓則悖也；外如拯溺救焚，所宜攘袂奮臂，而紓徐退遜則後也。中外奉法之臣，救偏葺敝，幾倖目前，而乏眞確乆遠之圖；守故襲常，攘譽嫁咎，而無協恭弘濟之實，豈不繆哉？

議者曰：「安內在擇吏。」是也。今郡縣之官，豈無廉平豈弟，如龔遂之在勃海、黃霸之在潁川、召信臣之在南陽、文翁之在蜀郡者乎？有之，未必盡陟；而貪鄙苟且、飾虛譽恡實惠者，或得以冒遷而規黜。此吏治之所以弗勸也。是故復乆任以固其志，精考課以稽其政，嚴舉刺以甄其類，公黜
translation_en:
…has not come to fulfillment. In frontier administration, officials are fettered by documentary formalities and regulations; idle procrastination has become habitual, and vigilance and preparedness are quite lax. There are the trappings of warfare and defense, but none of their substance: it is no wonder that military achievements have failed to flourish. Internal and external affairs have long depended upon one another. Without peace within, there is no means to exert the might needed to repel threats from without; unless external threats are repelled, there is no means to secure lasting peace within. Those who plan for the state certainly must not emphasize internal affairs while neglecting external ones; still less may they give urgency to external affairs while slighting internal ones. I have ventured to consider our present circumstances. Within, the task resembles supporting the weak and restoring the debilitated: what is needed is tranquil nourishment, rest, and recuperation; frantic exertion and exhaustion run counter to this purpose. Without, the task resembles rescuing the drowning and saving people from a fire: what is needed is to roll up one's sleeves and spring into action; delay and retreat will leave one too late. Officials charged with upholding the laws, both at court and in the provinces, remedy imbalances and patch up defects, hoping for good fortune in the immediate present but lacking sound and enduring plans. They cling to old practices and follow established routines, appropriating praise and shifting blame, without genuinely working together in respectful concord to accomplish great things. Is this not misguided?

Some argue: “Securing peace within depends upon selecting officials.” This is correct. Among today's prefectural and county officials, are there not men of integrity, fairness, and kindly disposition, like Gong Sui in Bohai, Huang Ba in Yingchuan, Shao Xinchen in Nanyang, and Wen Weng in Shu Commandery? Such men exist, yet they are not necessarily all promoted. Meanwhile, those who are greedy, base, and negligent, who embellish empty reputations while begrudging tangible benefits to the people, may contrive to obtain promotion and evade dismissal [?]. This is why good administration receives no encouragement. Therefore, restore long tenures to make officials steadfast in their intentions; refine performance evaluations to scrutinize their administration; make recommendations and censures rigorous to distinguish their respective kinds; be impartial in dismissals…

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:

得矣議者曰攘外在擇將是也今邊鄙之
將豈無知仁謀勇如魏尚之在雲中趙充
國之在湟中李廣之在上郡衞青之在上
谷者乎有之未必盡用而闇懦鮮耻張虚
捷隱實衊者或得以要賞而逭罰此士氣
之所以弗勵也是故精選舉以拔其才倡

以正其度其馭將之要務乎而良將可□□
===

異代謂才不如古者舛也振厲綜察之術
在加之意而已雖然治莫急于厚本幾莫

多事難以盡蠲而煩征羨役不有可省者

也雖屯鹽久弛庾帑時匱難以必充而積

陟，以示之典，其馭吏之要務乎？而良吏可得矣。議者曰：「攘外在擇將。」是也。今邊鄙之將，豈無知仁謀勇如魏尚之在雲中、趙充國之在湟中、李廣之在上郡、衞青之在上谷者乎？有之未必盡用，而闇懦鮮耻、張虚捷、隱實衊者，或得以要賞而逭罰，此士氣之所以弗勵也。是故精選舉以拔其才，倡勇敢以作其氣，授便宜以盡其能，辨功罪以正其度，其馭將之要務乎？而良將可□□矣。

夫天下未嘗無才，而致治未嘗借才于異代，謂才不如古者，舛也。振厲綜察之術，在加之意而已。雖然，治莫急于厚本，幾莫切于酌時，化莫要于審勢。今時勢日趨于文，而轉移莫急于本。夫民之所賴曰財與力，貴慎節而休逸之也。雖歲值凶荒，時當多事，難以盡蠲，而煩征羨役，不有可省者乎？兵之所資曰芻與餉，貴預處而充足之也。雖屯鹽久弛，庾帑時匱，難以必充，而積
translation_en:
…and promotions, to make the governing standards clear to them: is this not an essential task in managing officials? Good officials can thereby be obtained. Those who discuss the matter say, “Repelling external threats depends on choosing generals.” This is correct. Among the generals now serving on the frontiers, are there none possessing wisdom, benevolence, resourcefulness, and courage, like Wei Shang in Yunzhong, Zhao Chongguo in Huangzhong, Li Guang in Shangjun, and Wei Qing in Shanggu? Such men exist, yet they are not necessarily all employed. Meanwhile, the ignorant, cowardly, and shameless, who exaggerate fictitious victories and conceal actual disgrace [?], sometimes manage to secure rewards and escape punishment. This is why the soldiers’ morale is not roused. Thus, to exercise care in selection and recommendation so as to bring forward talent; to encourage bravery so as to stir their spirit; to grant discretion so that they may fully exercise their abilities; and to distinguish merit from wrongdoing so as to set the standards right—is this not an essential task in managing generals? Good generals can then [two illegible characters].

The world has never lacked talent, nor has achieving good government ever required borrowing talented men from another age. To say that present talent falls short of that of antiquity is mistaken. The methods of spurring men to exert themselves and comprehensively assessing them require only that attention be devoted to them. Nevertheless, in government nothing is more urgent than strengthening the foundations; in responding to incipient developments, nothing is more pressing than weighing the circumstances of the time; and in bringing about transformation, nothing is more essential than examining prevailing tendencies. Today, prevailing circumstances tend increasingly toward outward forms, and nothing is more urgent for changing this course than attending to the foundations. What the people depend upon is their wealth and strength: the essential thing is to use these sparingly and cautiously and allow the people rest. Although years of famine and times of many troubles make it difficult to remit all exactions, are there not burdensome levies and excessive labor services that could be reduced? What the army depends upon is fodder and provisions: the essential thing is to arrange for these beforehand and ensure adequate supplies. Although the military agricultural colonies and the salt administration have long been neglected, and the granaries and treasuries are frequently depleted, making it difficult to ensure full supplies, yet accumulated…

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
貯冗冒不有可講者乎舍此不務而欲吏
之惠政及于民將之恩信結乎士雖日從
事于勸懲賞罰之間終亦文而已矣方今
聖天子在上百辟承式弘猷淵筭諒籌之審矣
又何假于芻蕘之言然葑菲之采固亦集
思廣益之道也惟進而教之幸甚
第三問
劉璞
同考試官學正吳批揚確古人學術事
===
功若鑑懸衡持可以爲儒矣
考試官右中允孫批引援今昔評隲不苟其
識見素定者耶
考試官侍讀郭批品藻明確非漫然隨衆者
士生千載之下而論人于千載之上亦曰
揆諸聖以折其衷權其時以盡其變而已
矣夫聖道之準也時事之因也弗揆諸聖

translation_en:
…storage, superfluous expenditures, and fraudulent claims: are there not matters here that warrant consideration? If these concerns are neglected, yet one hopes that officials’ benevolent administration will reach the people and that commanders’ kindness and trustworthiness will bind their soldiers to them, then even daily efforts at encouragement and correction, rewards and punishments, will ultimately amount to mere outward form. Now the sagely Son of Heaven reigns above, and the assembled officials follow his example. Surely his grand plans and profound calculations have weighed these matters thoroughly. What need, then, is there for the words of a grass-cutter or wood-gatherer? Yet gathering even turnips and radishes—that is, accepting humble contributions—is indeed a way of pooling ideas for greater benefit. If you would offer me further instruction, I would be most fortunate.
Third Question
Liu Pu
Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, School Instructor: “He elucidates and establishes [?] the learning and practical achievements of the ancients, as though suspending a mirror and holding a balance. He may be counted a Confucian scholar.”
Comment by Examiner Sun, Right Mentor: “He adduces examples from past and present, and his judgments are never careless. Surely his discernment has long been firmly established?”
Comment by Examiner Guo, Reader-in-Waiting: “His appraisals are clear and precise; he is no thoughtless follower of the crowd.”
For a scholar born a thousand years later to judge men who lived a thousand years before, the task is simply to measure them against the sages in order to reach a balanced judgment, and to weigh the circumstances of their times in order to comprehend the full range of variation. The sages are the standard of the Way; the times are the circumstances on which affairs depend. Without measuring men against the sages, how can one reach a balanced judgment amid the mingling of purity and flaws, excellence and inferiority? Without weighing their times, how can one fully comprehend the variations arising from their encounters with prosperity and decline, difficulty and ease? With discernment in these matters, one may perhaps…

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
乎藻鑑明而權衡審可以評隲古今而訂
確異論矣夫景附而聲和者哲人之所羞
也瘢索而疵求者拘士之所執也慨自光
岳氣分世無全才聖遠言湮士鮮實學伊
周之事業孔孟之學術戰國而後追蹤振
嚮者固稱尠矣然近似者尚可續如綫之
傳而暗合者猶能揚餘光之耀烏可以世
降時移而遽謂懸異也耶是故以學術言
之于漢吾得一人焉曰董江都于隋吾得
===
一人焉曰王仲淹于唐吾得一人焉曰韓
昌黎夫潛心大業而天人三策淵乎格君
之謨罷黜百家而道誼數言亶哉拯世之
論舒固一代醇儒也災異事應未免拘泥
之過要亦有見而然爾程子稱其度越諸
子而真氏稱其有功學者其品藻之公乎
兩相驕主正身率物秦漢而下豈有出其
右者哉邦欲昌則獻策以匡時庶幾東周
之心時弗庸則隱居以授學卓乎卷懷之

punctuated: 乎藻鑑明而權衡審，可以評隲古今而訂確異論矣。夫景附而聲和者，哲人之所羞也；瘢索而疵求者，拘士之所執也。慨自光岳氣分，世無全才，聖遠言湮，士鮮實學。伊周之事業，孔孟之學術，戰國而後，追蹤振嚮者固稱尠矣。然近似者尚可續如綫之傳，而暗合者猶能揚餘光之耀，烏可以世降時移而遽謂懸異也耶？是故以學術言之，于漢吾得一人焉，曰董江都；于隋吾得一人焉，曰王仲淹；于唐吾得一人焉，曰韓昌黎。夫潛心大業，而天人三策，淵乎格君之謨；罷黜百家，而道誼數言，亶哉拯世之論。舒固一代醇儒也。災異事應，未免拘泥之過，要亦有見而然爾。程子稱其度越諸子，而真氏稱其有功學者，其品藻之公乎？兩相驕主，正身率物，秦漢而下，豈有出其右者哉？邦欲昌，則獻策以匡時，庶幾東周之心；時弗庸，則隱居以授學，卓乎卷懷之
translation_en:
…one may achieve clear discernment and sound judgment, assess men of antiquity and the present, and settle divergent opinions. To attach oneself like a shadow and echo another’s voice is what the wise find shameful; to search for scars and seek out faults is the fixation of narrow-minded scholars. Alas, since the vital energies of the heavens and mountains became divided, the world has lacked men of complete talent; with the sages distant and their words obscured, few scholars possess substantive learning. Since the Warring States period, those who have followed in the footsteps and carried forward the influence of the achievements of Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou, or the learning of Confucius and Mencius, have indeed been few. Yet those who approximate them can still continue a threadlike transmission, and those who accord with them unwittingly can still spread the brilliance of their lingering light. How, merely because the ages have declined and times have changed, can one hastily declare them utterly different?
Thus, speaking of learning, in the Han I find one man: Dong of Jiangdu; in the Sui I find one man: Wang Zhongyan; in the Tang I find one man: Han of Changli. Devoting himself to the great undertaking, Dong offered his Three Policy Responses on Heaven and Man: profound were his plans for rectifying the ruler! Rejecting the Hundred Schools, he spoke briefly of the Way and righteousness: truly these were arguments for saving the age. Dong Zhongshu was certainly a Confucian of pure learning in his generation. His treatment of calamities and anomalies as corresponding to human affairs was not free from excessive rigidity, yet it arose from insights of his own. Master Cheng praised him as surpassing the various masters, and Master Zhen praised his service to those who study: were these not impartial assessments? Twice serving as chancellor to arrogant princes, he set himself upright and led others by example. Since the Qin and Han, who could surpass him?
When the state was about to flourish, Wang presented policies to set the age right, approaching Confucius’s aspiration to make an Eastern Zhou. When the times afforded him no employment, he withdrew to teach, lofty in his resolve to fold away and conceal his talents…

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
志通寔一時傑儒也續經中說雖未免儗
聖之迹要非漫然而為者朱子譏其妄也
而至比以吳楚僭王無乃誅絕之甚乎醇
詞典訓多所發明晋隋之際其罕若人之
儔哉若夫昌黎當士風波靡之時衆言淆
亂之後原道一篇文起八代之衰佛骨一
表道濟天下之溺闢邪翼正彷彿孟氏家
法也浮華之習利達之求君子譏焉固也
夫學以自得為真行以大節為尚取其美
===
而略其疵則昌黎之學蓋已識其大者韓
其振世之豪傑也乎以事功言之于漢吾
得一人焉曰張留侯于三國吾得一人焉
曰諸葛武侯于唐吾得一人焉曰狄梁公
夫運籌帷幄而潜伸為韓之謀因事納忠
而佐成炎漢之業子房之功大矣四皓之
招納約自牖之忠也赤松之游明哲保身
之智也南軒稱其有儒者氣象誠非溢美
世徒迹其始終為韓也而專以智術目之

亂之後原道一篇文起八代之衰佛骨一
表道濟天下之溺闢邪翼正彷彿孟氏家
法也浮華之習利達之求君子譏焉固也
大學以自得爲眞行以大節爲尚取其美
===
而略其疵則昌黎之學蓋已識其大者韓
其振世之豪傑也乎以事功言之于漢吾
得一人焉曰張留侯于三國吾得一人焉
曰諸葛武侯于唐吾得一人焉曰狄梁公
夫運籌帷幄而潛伸爲韓之謀因事納忠
而佐成炎漢之業子房之功大矣四皓之
招納約自牖之忠也赤松之游明哲保身
之智也南軒稱其有儒者氣象誠非溢美
世徒迹其始終爲韓也而專以智術目之
punctuated:
志。通寔一時傑儒也。《續經》《中說》雖未免儗聖之迹，要非漫然而為者。朱子譏其妄也，而至比以吳楚僭王，無乃誅絕之甚乎？醇詞典訓，多所發明，晋隋之際，其罕若人之儔哉！若夫昌黎，當士風波靡之時、衆言淆亂之後，《原道》一篇，文起八代之衰；《佛骨》一表，道濟天下之溺。闢邪翼正，彷彿孟氏家法也。浮華之習，利達之求，君子譏焉，固也。夫學以自得為真，行以大節為尚，取其美而略其疵，則昌黎之學蓋已識其大者。韓其振世之豪傑也乎！
以事功言之，于漢吾得一人焉，曰張留侯；于三國吾得一人焉，曰諸葛武侯；于唐吾得一人焉，曰狄梁公。夫運籌帷幄，而潜伸為韓之謀；因事納忠，而佐成炎漢之業，子房之功大矣！四皓之招，納約自牖之忠也；赤松之游，明哲保身之智也。南軒稱其有儒者氣象，誠非溢美。世徒迹其始終為韓也，而專以智術目之，
translation_en:
…aspiration. Wang Tong was indeed an outstanding Confucian of his age. Although his Continuations of the Classics (Xu jing) and Explanations of the Mean (Zhong shuo) inevitably bore traces of emulating the Sage, they were by no means carelessly undertaken. Master Zhu criticized his presumption, going so far as to compare him to the rulers of Wu and Chu who usurped the title of king. Was this not excessively harsh condemnation? His pure language and authoritative teachings elucidated much. In the age spanning Jin and Sui, how rare were men of his kind!
As for Han Yu of Changli, he lived when the ethos of scholars drifted with the current, after contending doctrines had sown confusion. With a single essay, Inquiry into the Way, he revived literary writing from the decline of eight dynasties; with a single memorial, On the Buddha’s Bone, he used the Way to rescue the drowning world. In rejecting heterodoxy and supporting orthodoxy, he resembled the school of Mencius. That gentlemen should criticize his tendency toward ornate display and his pursuit of profit and advancement is certainly proper. Yet learning is genuine when its insights are personally attained, and conduct is valued for integrity in great matters. If we accept his merits and overlook his flaws, Changli’s learning surely shows that he grasped what was essential. Was Han Yu not a heroic figure who roused his age?
In terms of practical achievements, I find one man in the Han: Zhang Liang, Marquis of Liu; one in the Three Kingdoms: Zhuge Liang, Marquis of Wu; and one in the Tang: Di Renjie, Duke of Liang. Planning strategy within the command tent, Zhang Liang secretly advanced his designs on behalf of the state of Han; offering loyal counsel as circumstances arose, he helped establish the imperial enterprise of the fire-virtue Han dynasty. Great indeed were the achievements of Zifang, as Zhang Liang was styled! His summoning of the Four Hoary Elders exemplified the loyalty of one who ‘offers simple pledges through the window’—counsel conveyed through a receptive opening. His roaming with Master Chisong exemplified the wisdom of discerning men who preserve themselves. Nanxuan’s praise of him as possessing the bearing of a Confucian was truly no exaggeration. People merely trace his service to the state of Han from beginning to end and regard him exclusively as a practitioner of cunning stratagems…

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
淺矣哉隆中三顧得出處之中行出師二
表明漢賊之大義孔明之事偉矣開誠布
公蹇蹇匪躬之節也寧靜致遠禮樂可興
之具也程子稱其有王佐才誠爲篤論世
徒因其志決身殲也而卽以成敗較之末
矣哉若夫梁公當唐祚旣移之際虐焰方
熾之期委蛇艱險終持主器之重潛授才
賢卒收夾日之功謀猷論議庶幾聖賢作
用也委質周朝屈身女主世俗議焉非也
===
夫道以達幾爲權功以識時爲智周其仕
而唐其心梁公之所遭蓋有獨當其難者
狄其濟變之大忠也乎嗚呼衆蔽而獨明
之也難羣倡而往和之也易處常而順應
也易當變而克濟也難數子者蓋當其難
而值其變者也後人不察而槩訾之曰三
代以下人物未聞道也無乃決衡之論與
然此卽執事所問者言之耳若夫濂洛關
閩之學獨得其宗韓范司馬之勛輝映千

閩之學獨得其宗韓范司馬之勛輝耿于
punctuated:
淺矣哉！隆中三顧，得出處之中行；出師二表，明漢賊之大義。孔明之事偉矣！開誠布公，蹇蹇匪躬之節也；寧靜致遠，禮樂可興之具也。程子稱其有王佐才，誠爲篤論。世徒因其志決身殲也，而卽以成敗較之，末矣哉！若夫梁公當唐祚旣移之際、虐焰方熾之期，委蛇艱險，終持主器之重；潛授才賢，卒收夾日之功。謀猷論議，庶幾聖賢作用也。委質周朝，屈身女主，世俗議焉，非也。
夫道以達幾爲權，功以識時爲智。周其仕而唐其心，梁公之所遭，蓋有獨當其難者。狄其濟變之大忠也乎！嗚呼！衆蔽而獨明之也難，羣倡而往和之也易；處常而順應也易，當變而克濟也難。數子者，蓋當其難而值其變者也。後人不察而槩訾之曰：「三代以下人物，未聞道也。」無乃決衡之論與？然此卽執事所問者言之耳。若夫濂洛關閩之學，獨得其宗；韓范司馬之勛，輝映千
translation_en:
…How shallow! When Kongming received the three visits at Longzhong, he struck the proper balance between taking office and remaining in retirement; in his two Memorials on Dispatching the Army, he clarified the great moral distinction between the Han and its usurpers. How magnificent were Kongming’s deeds! His openness and impartiality manifested the integrity of one who labored steadfastly without regard for himself; his tranquility and far-reaching purpose equipped him to revive rites and music. Master Cheng called him a man with the talent to assist a true king: this was indeed a sound judgment. Yet people merely seize upon his having died with his resolve unfulfilled and assess him solely by success or failure. How superficial! As for the Duke of Liang, at a time when the Tang throne had already passed into other hands and the flames of tyranny were blazing, he maneuvered through peril and adversity, ultimately upholding the weighty claims of the rightful heir. He quietly advanced talented and worthy men and finally achieved the merit of supporting the imperial sun. His plans and deliberations approached the practical achievements of sages and worthies. Common opinion censures him for pledging service to the Zhou court and bowing before a female ruler. This is mistaken.
In practicing the Way, expedient judgment consists in discerning the incipient tendencies of events; in achieving results, wisdom consists in understanding the times. His service was to Zhou, but his heart belonged to Tang. In what the Duke of Liang encountered, there were surely difficulties that he alone had to shoulder. Was not Di a man of supreme loyalty who steered the state through upheaval? Alas! To see clearly alone when the multitude is blinded is difficult; to join in when the crowd raises its voice is easy. To respond suitably under ordinary circumstances is easy; to meet upheaval and successfully bring matters through is difficult. These men faced precisely such difficulties and encountered precisely such upheavals. Later generations, failing to examine their circumstances, indiscriminately disparage them, saying: “The men who lived after the Three Dynasties had never heard the Way.” Is this not a judgment made with a faulty balance [?]? Yet I have spoken here only of those about whom you asked. As for the learning of Lian, Luo, Guan, and Min, which alone grasped its essential tradition, and the achievements of Han, Fan, and Sima, whose brilliance shines through a thousand …

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
策而明問弗之及者豈非以一當道學大
明之時一當君臣相與之盛無俟于論述
也耶微顯而闡幽執事之意深矣夫論事
貴盡而取人貴恕盡則人識中正之極而
弗畫於小成恕則人勵偏長之善而弗甘
於自棄古今之通義也然時之所值則有
不可强者此傑人志士恒以爲難而毎興
慨嘆也夫茍遭時之盛矣而不能振拔以
圖建立于世自棄孰甚焉此固執事未發
===
之意承學竊有志而未能者也不識執事
有取於愚言否乎
第四問
袁洪愈
同考試官教諭鄭批是作博極星學諸
書折衷經史獨究授時察變分職之義辨而有
紀約而甚章殆所謂知曆理者豈徒推驗之文
而已哉
同考試官學正蘇批考數而根理推天

策，而明問弗之及者，豈非以一當道學大明之時，一當君臣相與之盛，無俟于論述也耶？微顯而闡幽，執事之意深矣！夫論事貴盡，而取人貴恕。盡則人識中正之極，而弗畫於小成；恕則人勵偏長之善，而弗甘於自棄。古今之通義也。然時之所值，則有不可强者，此傑人志士恒以爲難，而毎興慨嘆也。夫茍遭時之盛矣，而不能振拔以圖建立于世，自棄孰甚焉？此固執事未發之意，承學竊有志而未能者也。不識執事有取於愚言否乎？

袁洪愈

translation_en:
…annals. Your illuminating question does not touch upon these men: is this not because the one group lived when the Learning of the Way shone brightly, and the other when cooperation between ruler and ministers flourished, so that no further discussion was needed? In drawing out subtleties in what is manifest and illuminating what is hidden, your intention is profound indeed!
In discussing affairs, one prizes thoroughness; in judging men, one prizes forbearance. Through thoroughness, people recognize the highest standard of balance and rectitude and do not stop at modest accomplishments. Through forbearance, people are encouraged to cultivate their particular strengths and do not resign themselves to giving up. This is a principle common to ancient and modern times. Yet the circumstances of the age one encounters cannot always be forced. Outstanding men and men of resolve have always found this difficult and have often sighed in lament. But if one encounters a flourishing age and still cannot rouse oneself to strive for accomplishments in the world, what greater self-abandonment could there be? This surely is the intention you have left unspoken. As a student, I privately aspire to fulfill it but have not yet succeeded. I do not know whether you will find anything worth accepting in my humble words.

Yuan Hongyu

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
而驗人其深知象緯之學者與
考試官右中允孫批象數悉陳而重於法序
分職儒者達天之學固如此
考試官侍讀郭批談天文事核義精無如
此作
君子之事天也有三義焉以授時者步其
數以察變者觀其文以分職者法其序數
不步則候氣測景之法不明推驗失真時
何以授文不觀則正儀立度之經不攷宿
離乖次變何以察序不法則順令舉事之
常不飭天人異感職何以分故堯典之曆
象言授時也而周官之馮相寔掌之舜典
之璣衡言察變也而周官之保章寔掌之
洪範之庶徵言分職也而周官之司會寔
掌之順以舉職職以應變變以從時時以
合天君子之事天也夫豈易言哉昔在先
王將步天路用定靈軌尋緒本原是故履
端立極體其元布政考績因其歲禮動樂

而驗人，其深知象緯之學者與！

考試官右中允孫批：象數悉陳，而重於法序分職，儒者達天之學固如此。

考試官侍讀郭批：談天文，事核義精，無如此作。

君子之事天也，有三義焉：以授時者步其數，以察變者觀其文，以分職者法其序。數不步，則候氣測景之法不明，推驗失真，時何以授？文不觀，則正儀立度之經不攷，宿離乖次，變何以察？序不法，則順令舉事之常不飭，天人異感，職何以分？故《堯典》之曆象，言授時也，而《周官》之馮相寔掌之；《舜典》之璣衡，言察變也，而《周官》之保章寔掌之；《洪範》之庶徵，言分職也，而《周官》之司會寔掌之。順以舉職，職以應變，變以從時，時以合天，君子之事天也，夫豈易言哉！昔在先王，將步天路，用定靈軌，尋緒本原。是故履端立極，體其元；布政考績，因其歲；禮動樂
translation_en:
…and tests it against human affairs. Surely he possesses a profound understanding of the study of celestial configurations!

Examiner Sun, Right Mentor, comments: He sets forth celestial configurations and numerical calculations comprehensively, while placing particular emphasis on taking celestial order as a model for allocating official responsibilities. Such indeed is the Confucian scholar’s learning for comprehending Heaven.

Examiner Guo, Reader-in-Waiting, comments: In discussing astronomy, no essay equals this one in the accuracy of its facts and the refinement of its meaning.

There are three principles by which the gentleman serves Heaven: to make the seasons known, he calculates its numerical cycles; to observe changes, he studies its patterns; and to allocate responsibilities, he takes its order as his model. Unless its cycles are calculated, the methods of observing seasonal influences and measuring shadows remain unclear, and calculations and verification lose their accuracy: how, then, can the seasons be made known? Unless its patterns are observed, the principles of aligning instruments and establishing measures go unexamined, and the positions of the lunar lodges depart from their proper sequence [?]: how, then, can changes be discerned? Unless its order is taken as a model, the regular practice of undertaking affairs in accordance with seasonal ordinances goes unregulated, and Heaven and humanity fail to respond in harmony: how, then, can responsibilities be allocated? Thus, the calendrical calculations and celestial observations in the Canon of Yao concern making the seasons known, and in the Offices of Zhou these are specifically entrusted to the Royal Astronomer. The celestial instrument and its transverse sighting tube in the Canon of Shun concern observing changes, and in the Offices of Zhou these are specifically entrusted to the Royal Astrologer. The various signs in the Great Plan concern allocating responsibilities, and in the Offices of Zhou these are specifically entrusted to the Grand Accountant. By following celestial order one discharges one’s duties; through those duties one responds to changes; through those changes one accords with the seasons; and through the seasons one harmonizes with Heaven. How could the gentleman’s service to Heaven be readily explained!

In ancient times, the former kings sought to calculate the paths of Heaven, thereby determining its numinous courses and tracing their threads back to their origins. Thus, in determining the beginning and establishing the standard, they embodied its primal inception; in promulgating government and assessing achievements, they followed its yearly cycle; in the operation of ritual and music…

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
和正其朔五行九伐順其氣庶政修明從
其日月顥顥乎稱爲有道之世王室衰微
諸侯力政史不紀時君不告朔是以疇人
分散洊致菑祲由此觀之達天明數有關
於治亂之大豈可假託以爲讖術廢黜而
不講乎漢藝文志所載天文二十一家自
泰壹星子經至圖書祕記凡四百四十五
卷眇含高遠總括幽玄其在度數之推者
則三百六十五日四分日之一日與天會
===
以分至啓閉定四時是爲一歲之紀二十
九日六辰有奇月與日會以晦朔弦朢定
大小是爲一月之紀十二辰繞地一匝以
晨昏出沒定脩短是爲一日之紀日臨卯
酉謂之分日正子午謂之至北至以後消
其積縮謂之啓南至以後消其積盈謂之
閉日舒月速當其同謂之合朔以速及舒
光盡體伏謂之晦舒先速後近一遠三謂
之弦相與爲衡分天之中謂之朢日氣修

大小是爲一月之紀十二辰繞地一匝以
晨昏出沒定脩短是爲一日之紀日臨卯
酉謂之分日正子午謂之至北至以後消
其積縮謂之啓南至以後消其積盈謂之
閉日舒月速當其同謂之合朔以速及舒
光盡體伏謂之晦舒先速後近一遠三謂
之弦相與爲衡分天之中謂之望日氣修
punctuated:
和，正其朔；五行九伐，順其氣；庶政修明，從其日月。顥顥乎，稱爲有道之世！王室衰微，諸侯力政，史不紀時，君不告朔，是以疇人分散，洊致菑祲。由此觀之，達天明數，有關於治亂之大，豈可假託以爲讖術，廢黜而不講乎？漢藝文志所載天文二十一家，自《泰壹星子經》至《圖書祕記》，凡四百四十五卷，眇含高遠，總括幽玄。

其在度數之推者，則三百六十五日四分日之一，日與天會，以分至啓閉定四時，是爲一歲之紀；二十九日六辰有奇，月與日會，以晦朔弦朢定大小，是爲一月之紀；十二辰繞地一匝，以晨昏出沒定脩短，是爲一日之紀。日臨卯酉，謂之分；日正子午，謂之至。北至以後，消其積縮，謂之啓；南至以後，消其積盈，謂之閉。日舒月速，當其同，謂之合朔；以速及舒，光盡體伏，謂之晦；舒先速後，近一遠三，謂之弦；相與爲衡，分天之中，謂之朢。日氣修
translation_en:
…with music brought into harmony, they set right the beginnings of the months; through the Five Phases and the nine kinds of punitive expedition, they accorded with celestial qi; with the various affairs of government cultivated and made clear, they followed the days and months. How radiant it was—a world acclaimed as possessing the Way! When the royal house declined, the feudal lords governed by force, the scribes ceased to record the seasons, and rulers ceased to perform the rites announcing the new moon. Consequently, the hereditary specialists in astronomy and calendrical reckoning scattered, and calamities and baleful portents repeatedly ensued. Seen in this light, understanding Heaven and comprehending its numerical patterns bear profoundly upon order and disorder. How could one dismiss these studies as arts of prophetic prognostication and abandon them without investigation? The “Treatise on Bibliography” in the History of the Han lists twenty-one schools of astronomy, from the Classic of Taiyi Xingzi [?] to the Secret Records of Diagrams and Writings, totaling 445 juan. Their subtle contents embrace what is lofty and distant and encompass what is hidden and mysterious.

As for calculations of celestial measures and numerical cycles: after 365 and one-quarter days, the sun returns to its corresponding position in the heavens. The equinoxes, solstices, and seasonal openings and closings establish the four seasons: this constitutes the cycle of a year. After twenty-nine days and six double-hours, with a remainder, the moon meets the sun. The last day of the lunar month, the new moon, the quarter moons, and the full moon determine the long and short months: this constitutes the cycle of a month. In twelve double-hours, a complete circuit is made around the earth; dawn and dusk, rising and setting determine the lengths of day and night: this constitutes the cycle of a day. When the sun reaches the mao and you positions, due east and west, this is called an equinox; when it aligns with zi and wu, due north and south, this is called a solstice. After its northern limit, its accumulated contraction is reduced: this is called the opening. After its southern limit, its accumulated excess is reduced: this is called the closing. The sun moves slowly and the moon swiftly; when their positions coincide, this is called conjunction at the new moon. When the swift catches up with the slow, the light is exhausted and the body concealed: this is called the dark moon. When the slow is ahead and the swift behind, with one part on the near side and three on the far side, this is called a quarter moon. When they face one another in balance, dividing the heavens through the middle, this is called the full moon. As for the length of daylight …

text:
短攠爲刻分以節晨昏以驗出沒此所謂
步數以授時者也事天之道也其在法象
之著者則日行天一日一周月行天一月
一周歲星之周天常以十二年塡星以二
十八年熒惑以二年惟辰星太白附日而
行或速則先日晨見於東或遲則後日昏
見於西故亦歲一周天此七政之大經也
紫微爲皇極之居太微爲五帝之座天市
爲下元之宮是曰三垣東方之宿蒼龍連
===
蜷於左西方之宿白虎雄踞於右南方之
宿朱雀奮翼於前北方之宿靈龜圈首於
後是曰二十八舍中外之官常明者百有
二十可名者三百二十爲星二千五百微
星萬一千五百二十庶物蠢動咸得繫節
經星因出沒以象占之緯星隨遲速以數
測之主客伏見凌守贏縮覈往占來歷示
休咎此所謂觀文以察變者也事天之道
也其在職事之符者仲春之月平秩東作

短攠爲刻分，以節晨昏，以驗出沒，此所謂步數以授時者也，事天之道也。
其在法象之著者，則日行天，一日一周；月行天，一月一周；歲星之周天，常以十二年；塡星以二十八年；熒惑以二年。惟辰星、太白附日而行，或速則先日，晨見於東；或遲則後日，昏見於西，故亦歲一周天。此七政之大經也。紫微爲皇極之居，太微爲五帝之座，天市爲下元之宮，是曰三垣。東方之宿，蒼龍連蜷於左；西方之宿，白虎雄踞於右；南方之宿，朱雀奮翼於前；北方之宿，靈龜圈首於後，是曰二十八舍。中外之官，常明者百有二十，可名者三百二十，爲星二千五百，微星萬一千五百二十。庶物蠢動，咸得繫節。經星因出沒以象占之，緯星隨遲速以數測之。主客伏見，凌守贏縮，覈往占來，歷示休咎，此所謂觀文以察變者也，事天之道也。
其在職事之符者，仲春之月，平秩東作，
translation_en:
…the varying length of daylight is apportioned [?] into quarter-hours and smaller divisions, to regulate dawn and dusk and verify rising and setting. This is what is meant by calculating celestial motions to announce the seasons; it is the way of serving Heaven.
As for what is manifest in celestial patterns and configurations, the sun makes one circuit of heaven in a day, and the moon one circuit in a month. Jupiter ordinarily completes its circuit in twelve years, Saturn in twenty-eight years, and Mars in two years. Mercury and Venus alone travel in attendance upon the sun: when faster, they precede it and appear in the east at dawn; when slower, they follow it and appear in the west at dusk. Thus they too complete one circuit of heaven each year. These are the principal regularities of the Seven Luminaries. Ziwei, the Purple Tenuity Enclosure, is the abode of the Imperial Ultimate; Taiwei, the Supreme Tenuity Enclosure, is the seat of the Five Emperors; and Tianshi, the Celestial Market Enclosure, is the palace of the Lower Origin. These are called the Three Enclosures. Among the eastern lunar lodges, the Azure Dragon coils along the left; among the western lodges, the White Tiger crouches majestically on the right; among the southern lodges, the Vermilion Bird spreads its wings in front; and among the northern lodges, the Numinous Tortoise curls its head behind. These are called the Twenty-Eight Lodges. Of the inner and outer celestial constellations, 120 are constantly visible and 320 can be named, comprising 2,500 stars; there are 11,520 faint stars. All the myriad creatures that stir and move are linked to the seasonal rhythms. The fixed stars are interpreted through their configurations as they rise and set; the planets are measured numerically according to the slowness or speed of their motion. The disappearance and appearance of regular and guest stars, encroachment and lingering, advance and retardation—all are used to examine the past and divine the future, successively revealing good and ill fortune. This is what is meant by observing celestial patterns to discern changes; it is the way of serving Heaven.
As for their correspondence with official duties, in the second month of spring, one duly orders the labors of the east…

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
厥民析則知日月會於降婁而爲奎婁之
次仲夏之月平秩南訛厥民因則知日月
會於鶉首而爲井鬼之次仲秋之月平秩
西成厥民夷則知日月會於壽星而爲角
亢之次仲冬之月平在朔易厥民隩則知
日月會於星紀而爲斗牛之次故歷代后
王尚之夏有少正周有時訓秦漢唐宋皆
有月令所以順時宜而督民務也詩曰定
之方中作于楚宮又有三星在天在隅在
===
戶之候春秋傳曰啟蟄而郊龍見而雩又
曰土功水昏正而栽又曰凡馬日中而出
日中而入所以視列宿而行國政也此所
謂法序以分職者也事天之道也是故時
無弗明以稽天數數則有準矣變無弗紀
以應天文文則有昭矣職無弗舉以循天
序序則有定矣上古太史之官察璣祥記
政令慎擇一人任之欽崇寅奉罔有愆違
乃後占候紀載析而爲二隳廢離隔不相

punctuated:
厥民析，則知日月會於降婁，而爲奎婁之次；仲夏之月，平秩南訛，厥民因，則知日月會於鶉首，而爲井鬼之次；仲秋之月，平秩西成，厥民夷，則知日月會於壽星，而爲角亢之次；仲冬之月，平在朔易，厥民隩，則知日月會於星紀，而爲斗牛之次。故歷代后王尚之，夏有少正，周有時訓，秦漢唐宋皆有月令，所以順時宜而督民務也。《詩》曰：「定之方中，作于楚宮。」又有三星在天、在隅、在戶之候。《春秋傳》曰：「啟蟄而郊，龍見而雩。」又曰：「土功，水昏正而栽。」又曰：「凡馬，日中而出，日中而入。」所以視列宿而行國政也。此所謂法序以分職者也，事天之道也。
是故時無弗明，以稽天數，數則有準矣；變無弗紀，以應天文，文則有昭矣；職無弗舉，以循天序，序則有定矣。上古太史之官，察璣祥，記政令，慎擇一人任之，欽崇寅奉，罔有愆違。乃後占候紀載，析而爲二，隳廢離隔，不相
translation_en:
…“the people disperse”: one thus knows that the sun and moon meet in Jianglou, the celestial station comprising the mansions Kui and Lou. In the middle month of summer, “orderly arrangements are made for the transformations of the south, and the people continue their labors”: one thus knows that the sun and moon meet in Chunshou, the station comprising Jing and Gui. In the middle month of autumn, “orderly arrangements are made for the completion of work in the west, and the people are at ease”: one thus knows that the sun and moon meet in Shouxing, the station comprising Jiao and Kang. In the middle month of winter, “due attention is given to the changes of the north, and the people shelter indoors”: one thus knows that the sun and moon meet in Xingji, the station comprising Dou and Niu. Thus the sovereigns of successive ages esteemed these practices. The Xia had the Lesser Rectifier (shaozheng), the Zhou had seasonal instructions, and the Qin, Han, Tang, and Song all had monthly ordinances, by which they followed the requirements of the seasons and supervised the people’s work. The Book of Odes says: “When Ding stood at the center of the sky, they built the palace at Chu.” It also gives indications of the seasons through the Three Stars being in the sky, at the corner, and at the doorway. The Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals says: “When hibernating creatures awaken, perform the suburban sacrifice; when the Dragon appears, perform the rain sacrifice.” It also says: “For earthworks, when the Water constellation culminates at dusk, set up the building frames.” It further says: “As a rule for horses, turn them out at the spring equinox and bring them in at the autumn equinox.” These are ways of observing the stellar mansions in conducting the government of the state. This is what is meant by taking the celestial order as a model for allocating duties; it is the way of serving Heaven.
Thus, when no season is left unclarified, so that Heaven’s numerical cycles may be examined, those cycles have a standard. When no anomaly is left unrecorded, so that Heaven’s patterns may be responded to, those patterns become manifest. When no duty is left unperformed, so that Heaven’s sequence may be followed, that sequence is settled. In high antiquity, the Grand Astrologer observed celestial signs [?] and recorded governmental commands. A single person was carefully selected for this responsibility; he honored it reverently and discharged it with solemn care, without error or deviation. Later, however, prognostication and observation on the one hand, and recording events on the other, were divided into two functions. They fell into neglect and became separated, no longer mutually …

text:
爲謀縑素委闐昏明交錯說者謂昆吾史
佚梓謹卜偃裨竈子韋唐昧尹臯諸所稱
述不如巫咸甘德石申雅善名數爲後代
所宗蓋三國時陳卓以三家星官著於圖
錄一時崇尚云爾何以稱焉故太史公曰
臯唐甘石因時務論書傳凌雜米鹽寔爲
確議要之演籌占候代有其人即今郭守
敬之遺亦稱脗合但諳曆理如楊雄不可
多得況又不爲楊雄者乎信乎非湛密
===

三五終始古今明時貞度斯謂經贊之績
斯於古者修德修救之道昭融符契矣
