爲謀，縑素委闐，昏明交錯。說者謂昆吾、史佚、梓謹、卜偃、裨竈、子韋、唐昧、尹臯諸所稱述，不如巫咸、甘德、石申雅善名數，爲後代所宗。蓋三國時陳卓以三家星官著於圖錄，一時崇尚云爾，何以稱焉？故太史公曰：「臯、唐、甘、石，因時務論，書傳凌雜米鹽。」寔爲確議。要之，演籌占候，代有其人。即今郭守敬之遺，亦稱脗合。但諳曆理如楊雄，不可多得，況又不爲楊雄者乎？信乎，非湛密弗能由，非明王弗能服聽。學士大夫必貫三五，終始古今，明時貞度，斯謂經贊之績，斯於古者修德修救之道昭融符契矣。
第五問
查光述
同考試官教諭楊批：「詞雄識高，深切時務，奇士也！高薦何忝？」
同考試官教諭潘批：「議論亹亹不窮，悉中肯綮，是經世之略也，錄之。」
translation_en:
…consult with one another. Written silks piled up in profusion, with obscurity and clarity intermingled. Commentators maintain that the accounts of Kunwu, Shi Yi, Zi Jin [?], Bu Yan, Bi Zao, Zi Wei, Tang Mei, and Yin Gao were inferior to those of Wu Xian, Gan De, and Shi Shen, who were especially proficient in nomenclature and numerical methods and were taken as authorities by later generations. Yet it was simply that, during the Three Kingdoms period, Chen Zhuo recorded the constellations of these three schools in charts and catalogues, and they enjoyed esteem at that time. On what grounds can such praise be justified? Thus the Grand Astrologer said: “Gao, Tang, Gan, and Shi discussed matters according to the needs of their times; their transmitted writings are a confused jumble of petty details.” This is indeed a sound judgment.
In sum, every age has had men who performed calculations with counting rods and observed celestial signs. Even now, the legacy of Guo Shoujing is said to accord with observed phenomena. But men who understand the principles of calendrical astronomy as Yang Xiong did are rare; how much less can be expected of those who do not measure up to Yang Xiong? Truly, only those of profound and meticulous understanding can pursue this way, and only an enlightened king can accept and heed them. Scholars and officials must comprehend the Three and the Five [?], encompass beginnings and endings, past and present, clarify the seasons, and set the measures aright. This is what constitutes achievement in ordering affairs and assisting the ruler; it accords clearly and fully with the ancients’ way of cultivating virtue and undertaking remedial action.
Fifth Policy Question
Zha Guangshu

text:
考試官右中允孫批抑揚頓挫音節鏗然當
是作者
考試官侍讀郭批敷答詳明文詞充暢可
以占所養矣
善天下之俗者端其習而已矣謹天下之
坊者守其法而已矣夫習之陂也其始若
無害而其積也則勢重而不可反法之立
也其始未嘗不行而其久也則怠弛而不
能振圖治者豈可使習陂而法弛也哉□
操感化之機者端習者也嚴振飭之節□
守法者也習端則善俗興法守則僞行戢
其明教化正風俗之要乎夫懷經久之圖
者廣忠益之謨抱先憂之志者不諱激切
之論執事以教化風俗發策下詢愚也伏
跡草野有感于衷久矣請爲執事誦之夫
教化者自上而率乎下者也風俗者成于
下而應乎上者也教化修而風俗正二者

Examiner Sun, Right Rectifier of the Heir Apparent, comments: “With its rises and falls, pauses and turns, its cadence rings out resonantly. This is surely the work of an accomplished writer.”
Examiner Guo, Expositor-in-waiting, comments: “The response is detailed and clear, its language ample and fluent. From it one can discern the writer’s cultivation.”
To improve the customs of the realm is simply to rectify its habits; to maintain carefully the realm’s moral barriers is simply to uphold its laws. When habits become corrupt, at first they seem harmless; but as their effects accumulate, their force becomes so great that it cannot be reversed. When laws are established, they are indeed enforced at first; but as time passes, enforcement grows lax and cannot be reinvigorated. How could those who seek good government allow habits to become corrupt and laws to fall into neglect? [Illegible character] Those who wield the means of moral transformation rectify habits; those who rigorously enforce measures of discipline [?] uphold the laws. When habits are rectified, good customs flourish; when laws are upheld, deceitful conduct is checked. Is this not the essential means of making moral instruction clear and setting customs right?
Those who cherish plans for enduring government welcome a broad range of loyal and beneficial counsel; those resolved to take thought for troubles before others do do not shun impassioned and forthright arguments. You, sir, have issued a policy question on moral instruction and customs, seeking counsel from those below. I, in my ignorance, have long lived in rural obscurity and have long felt deeply about these matters. Allow me to set them forth for you.
Moral instruction proceeds from those above to guide those below; customs take shape among those below and respond to those above. When moral instruction is cultivated, customs become upright: the two invariably depend upon each other. In the age of the sage kings of old, they cultivated the six rites to regulate the people’s dispositions …

translation_en:
…clarified the seven teachings to foster the people’s virtue, regulated the eight affairs of government to prevent excess, unified moral principles to bring customs into agreement, exalted the worthy to honor virtue, and distinguished the unworthy to suppress evil. At that time, prevailing habits were simple and sincere, and people’s hearts were honest and upright. Officials fulfilled their duties, and the people pursued their livelihoods in peace. Scholars engaged in no deviant conduct, and the realm had no idle wanderers. Those who failed to conform were punished by the responsible authorities and banished to distant borderlands, lest they corrupt the common people. Thus everyone cherished benevolence and delighted in righteousness, valued their own integrity, and felt ashamed to violate the law. How lofty and unsurpassable was the flourishing age of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties! From the decline of Zhou onward, the way of the true kings faded and hegemons arose; prevailing habits lost their sincerity and customs deteriorated. Although subsequent enlightened rulers and righteous sovereigns professed to seek good government, their transformation of the people did not accord with ancient standards. The decline of moral instruction has a long history indeed!
Our imperial ancestor rose vigorously when his destined time arrived, drove out the barbarian scourge, swept away that foul atmosphere, and established our Chinese rites. His teachings shone forth [?], and laws and institutions were fully provided. In those founding days, after the wars, prevailing habits returned to simplicity and sincerity. People were honest and feared the law; the population had not yet multiplied, and treachery and deceit did not arise. Successive sage emperors carried on his legacy, adapting institutions to benefit the people and extending moral transformation as they sat in dignified repose with hands folded. Yet after prolonged peace, people grew lax and heedless. Laws and ordinances became ever more numerous, while treachery and deceit increased daily.
Our sage sovereign has brought about a restoration. Seeing deeply into the sources of these abuses, he has further honored the foundations of moral transformation. He composed the Admonition on Reverent Unity (Jingyi) to admonish officials and people, regulated the suburban and ancestral temple sacrifices to rectify canonical ritual, made the rules for selection and assessment strict, and gave greater weight to examination in the learning of the Classics. …are subject to prescribed forms, and extravagance is prohibited. Regulations have been revised to remedy abuses, and false accusations punished to bring peace to the people. Such generous magnanimity and enlightened accomplishment truly suffice to match high antiquity and restore the old order of the imperial ancestors. If above there is a ruler who extends moral transformation, but below there are no ministers who propagate it, they are no worthy ministers. If above there is a sage who bestows the supreme standard, but below there are no people who uphold it, they are no worthy people. Officials and subjects at court and throughout the realm should therefore purify their intentions, reverently receive these teachings, and together attain a state of moral transformation.

In recent years [□: unclear], conditions have gradually come to differ somewhat from those at the outset. There are certainly many loyal and worthy ministers who serve the public, diligently discharge their duties, exercise restraint [□: unclear], and cherish the people. Yet not a few harbor greedy and base intentions, satisfy desires as bottomless as ravines, skillfully cover up their failings to escape punishment, and accept deprivation of rank without shame. There are certainly outstanding scholars who recite and emulate the sages and worthies and devote themselves to classical learning. Yet there are also those who craft obscure and ornate prose [?] in pursuit of superficial brilliance, pilfer scraps of Chan awakening [?] to devise arguments taking their own minds as authority, and whose words do not accord with their conduct and whose service yields little practical benefit.

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
衢路日盛月新禁不能止非所以重等威
一制度也頻年水旱荒歉甚矣而閭閻爭
以侈靡相高富者欲過貧者欲及殫室糜
財莫之知恤民之所以益貧乏也中外行
事多以簿書期會獵虛聲而忘實政文案
充積則官不能稽奸吏得緣法而遂私求
四方狡偽之眾飾浮詞以聳聽聞廣牽摭
以戕善良羣附黨和冀售其欺因以行罔
利之術此奸黠之風不可長也夫
===
聖明在上乾剛之德日照月臨巽命之行雷動
飈發而風俗若茲者良以沿襲之過奉行
德意之未至耳竊見邇來士習以容忍姑息為
德以疏通變譎為才病謹禮為木札謂守
正為滯著察瑣節而昧大體崇虛譽而略
實行此非所以揚熈皞之風廣敦厚之化
也嚴黜陟矣而倖塗漏網尚存也振風紀
矣而舉刺未盡協乎激揚之實也重經術
矣而未能黜浮崇雅也禁異服革奢僣懲

衢路，日盛月新，禁不能止，非所以重等威、一制度也。頻年水旱，荒歉甚矣，而閭閻爭以侈靡相高，富者欲過，貧者欲及，殫室糜財，莫之知恤，民之所以益貧乏也。中外行事，多以簿書期會獵虛聲而忘實政，文案充積，則官不能稽，奸吏得緣法而遂私求。四方狡偽之眾，飾浮詞以聳聽聞，廣牽摭以戕善良，羣附黨和，冀售其欺，因以行罔利之術，此奸黠之風不可長也。
夫聖明在上，乾剛之德日照月臨，巽命之行雷動飈發，而風俗若茲者，良以沿襲之過、奉行德意之未至耳。竊見邇來士習，以容忍姑息為德，以疏通變譎為才，病謹禮為木札，謂守正為滯著，察瑣節而昧大體，崇虛譽而略實行，此非所以揚熈皞之風、廣敦厚之化也。嚴黜陟矣，而倖塗漏網尚存也；振風紀矣，而舉刺未盡協乎激揚之實也；重經術矣，而未能黜浮崇雅也；禁異服、革奢僣、懲

…the thoroughfares, growing more prevalent by the day and changing by the month; prohibitions cannot stop them. This is no way to uphold distinctions of rank and authority or make regulations uniform. Floods and droughts in successive years have brought severe crop failures, yet ordinary households compete in extravagance: the rich wish to surpass others, and the poor wish to keep pace. They exhaust their households’ resources and squander their wealth, with no thought of conserving it. This is why the people become ever poorer. In conducting affairs, officials at court and in the provinces mostly seek empty acclaim through registers, paperwork, and reporting deadlines, forgetting substantive governance. Documents pile up beyond officials’ capacity to check them, and unscrupulous clerks exploit the law to satisfy their private demands. Cunning and deceitful people everywhere embellish specious statements to startle their hearers, indiscriminately implicate others and dredge up accusations to harm the innocent, and form factions that echo one another, hoping to make their deceit succeed. They thereby practice their arts of fraudulent gain. This tendency toward cunning dishonesty must not be allowed to grow.
Now the sagely and enlightened sovereign reigns above. His virtue, firm as Heaven, shines like the sun and watches over all like the moon; his commands, penetrating like the wind, take effect like thunder and the rising gale. That customs should nevertheless be like this is surely due to the fault of following entrenched practices and to the failure to carry out fully his virtuous intentions. I humbly observe that scholars’ habits of late have been to regard indulgence and appeasement as virtue, and facility and shifting guile as talent. They disparage scrupulous observance of ritual as wooden rigidity [?] and call adherence to rectitude obstinate inflexibility. They scrutinize trifling details while remaining blind to larger principles, and prize empty reputation while neglecting actual conduct. This is no way to foster customs of harmony and contentment or extend the transforming influence of sincerity and generosity. Demotions and promotions have been made strict, yet avenues to advancement by undeserved favor and loopholes still remain. Official discipline has been strengthened, yet recommendations and impeachments still do not fully serve the actual purpose of discouraging evil and encouraging good. Classical learning has been honored, yet frivolity has still not been rejected and refinement exalted. Outlandish dress has been prohibited, extravagance and usurpation of the privileges of rank have been curbed, and punishment…

title: 嘉靖二十五年應天府鄉試錄
text:
訐訟矣而申飭者之作輟也至於吏弊愈
過愈滋付之慨嘆而已所以致今日之風
俗可謂無其故乎是在端揆風紀奉法任
事之臣協心同德力挽而亟還之耳是故
操感化之機嚴振飭之節以宣
德意以明
舊章以變近時之積習此急務也布公道倡清
議以正其趨獎廉節重循良以堅其守崇
經學黜浮詭以辨其志躬節儉嚴等威以
===
導其從明職掌省繁文以覈其實厲法禁
公聽察以遏其源嚴貪吏之罰重風教之
官用守法之吏本之以公協之以誠行之
以信持之以乆則風俗庶幾其可正乎不
此之務而顧諉曰積習之難革風俗之難
正則非愚之所及知也狂瞽之言不識忌
諱惟執事擇焉

公聽察以遏其源嚴貪吏之罰重風教之
官用守法之吏本之以公協之以誠行之
以信持之以久則風俗庶幾其可正乎不
此之務而顧諉曰積習之難革風俗之難
正則非愚之所及知也狂瞽之言不識忌
諱惟執事擇焉
punctuated: 訐訟矣，而申飭者之作輟也。至於吏弊，愈過愈滋，付之慨嘆而已。所以致今日之風俗，可謂無其故乎？是在端揆、風紀、奉法任事之臣，協心同德，力挽而亟還之耳。是故操感化之機，嚴振飭之節，以宣德意，以明舊章，以變近時之積習，此急務也。布公道，倡清議，以正其趨；獎廉節，重循良，以堅其守；崇經學，黜浮詭，以辨其志；躬節儉，嚴等威，以導其從；明職掌，省繁文，以覈其實；厲法禁，公聽察，以遏其源。嚴貪吏之罰，重風教之官，用守法之吏，本之以公，協之以誠，行之以信，持之以乆，則風俗庶幾其可正乎？不此之務，而顧諉曰積習之難革、風俗之難正，則非愚之所及知也。狂瞽之言，不識忌諱，惟執事擇焉。
translation_en:
…malicious litigation has been punished, yet those charged with enforcing these injunctions act only intermittently. As for abuses among officials, they grow ever more numerous as time passes, and are met with sighs of regret alone. Can it be said that the present state of customs has arisen without cause? It rests with the chief councillors, the officials responsible for disciplinary surveillance, and the ministers charged with upholding the law and conducting affairs to unite in purpose and virtue, exert themselves to reverse this trend, and promptly restore proper customs.

Thus, to grasp the means of moral transformation and rigorously enforce measures of reform, thereby making known the imperial benevolent intentions, clarifying the established statutes, and changing the ingrained habits of recent times—this is the urgent task. Extend impartial principles and promote upright public judgment to set people's inclinations right; reward integrity and esteem conscientious, benevolent officials to strengthen their resolve; honor classical learning and reject superficiality and deceit to clarify their aspirations; personally practice frugality and strictly maintain distinctions of rank to guide those who follow; clarify official responsibilities and reduce excessive formalities to examine actual performance; enforce legal prohibitions and hear and investigate cases impartially to cut off abuses at their source. Punish corrupt officials severely, give due weight to officials responsible for moral instruction, and employ officials who observe the law. Ground these efforts in impartiality, unite them through sincerity, carry them out with good faith, and sustain them over time: might customs then be set right?

If, instead of attending to these tasks, one makes excuses, saying that ingrained habits are difficult to change and customs difficult to rectify, that is beyond my poor understanding. These rash and uninformed words take no account of taboos; I ask only that you, honored examiners, select what is worth accepting.

translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination

In the autumn of the bingwu year of Jiajing [1546], we, your servants Pu and Jie, reverently received the imperial command to preside over the examination in the Southern Metropolitan Region. Having taken leave of Your Majesty, we departed and traveled by water through Tianjin. We gazed toward the imperial palace, standing majestically at the northern pole, while east of the Taihang Mountains and west of Daizong [Mount Tai], the famous rivers converged and wound their way down to the sea. Together we exclaimed: “Ah, how magnificent! This is the achievement of Emperor Wen in choosing and establishing his capital—what is meant by strengthening the trunk and weakening the branches, exalting the supreme capital and looking out over the myriad states.”

Then we followed the course of the long Huai River and crossed the great Yangzi, that defensive moat. The strategic advantages and scenic grandeur of the southeast converge at Jinling: Zhongfu and Shicheng stand like a coiling dragon and a crouching tiger. We exclaimed: “Ah, how grand and splendid! This is the foundation laid by Emperor Gao at the dynasty’s founding—what is called the richest land of the Nine Provinces, the sheltered recess of Heaven and Earth.” The Book of Odes says: “The sacred mountain sent down its divine power …

translation_en:
…gave birth to Fu and Shen.” Thus, already at this point, one could foresee the gathering and concentration of talent here. Upon entering the examination compound, we assembled the many candidates and examined them in three sessions, selecting and ranking their compositions. These generally succeeded in revealing the profundities of human nature and destiny, comprehending what was appropriate in both ancient and modern times, and fully exploring the variations of human feelings and the principles of things. Their language was expansive and abundant, their spirit flourishing and grand, and their thought vast and profound. Their words were clear, their meanings subtle, and they accorded with canonical standards. Then we exclaimed once more: “How splendid! This is the achievement of the sagely Son of Heaven in nurturing men of talent—what is meant by ‘The many admirable men of talent are born in this royal realm.’” Yet the mountains and rivers, too, have contributed. As for the northern metropolitan region, reached by the exemplary influence of the capital and endowed with concentrated spiritual distinction, its abundance of cultivated men of letters can readily be imagined.

Formerly, when Ban Gu composed the Rhapsodies on the Two Capitals, he proudly extolled the beauty of their courts and marketplaces and the strength of the rivers and mountains protecting their borders, and celebrated the abundance of their revenues, ultimately turning to the literary attendants’ dignified …

translation_en: …with graceful praise, which he deemed sufficient to embellish the dynasty’s grand achievements. He went on to describe the ministers who assisted the ruler: their accomplishments were inscribed on bronze ritual vessels, their beneficence extended to the common people, and their good renown endured without end. Our dynasty has reached the height of its flourishing fortunes, with its two capitals standing side by side. Its territory and regional products surpass those of preceding dynasties. For more than one hundred and seventy years, its brilliant cultural accomplishments and consummate governance have manifestly shared the spirit of the Three Dynasties. Throughout this time, worthy men who supported the imperial mandate and assisted in government, advancing the state’s plans and bringing lustre to the emperor’s undertakings, have succeeded one another, illuminating the historical records. Could this be merely what Ban Gu celebrated in his rhapsodies? Moreover, this region truly preserves the legacy of nurturing talent, evoked by the luxuriant millet in the Odes; compared with the outlying territories, it received these blessings first. Surely it is fitting that men of outstanding and exceptional ability, like Fu and Shen, should emerge …

translation_en:
…among them. Now, in assessing the examination writings, we must be impartial and scrupulous, pledging ourselves to this task day and night, so as to find such men and enable them in due course to advance to official positions and together bring about our Emperor’s resurgent age of good government. Then those presiding over the examination will thereby gain honor, and even the mountains and rivers will acquire added splendor. I, your servant Sheng, have written this preface on the concluding leaves in fulfillment of my official duties, placing great hopes in the assembled scholars. May you scholars diligently and reverently apply yourselves!

Preface respectfully written by Sun Sheng, Right Mentor of the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent.
